POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:22:46 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.10 Philippe, Glucksmann, Retailleau : les temps forts du Sommet sur la compétitivité économique de POLITICO https://www.politico.eu/article/philippe-glucksmann-retailleau-les-temps-forts-du-sommet-sur-la-competitivite-economique-de-politico/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:00:25 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9154085 PARIS — Un peu plus de deux semaines après le Playbook Paris Live, où Gabriel Attal, Marine Le Pen et Jean-Luc Mélenchon étaient reçus, trois autres candidats à la présidentielle étaient invités à s’exprimer ce mardi sur les enjeux économiques du moment lors du Sommet sur la compétitivité économique de POLITICO.

Voitures thermiques et droits de douane

Avec l’ouverture du Salon de l’Auto, c’est l’un des sujets d’actu du jour : l’interdiction de la vente des voitures à moteur thermique dans l’Union européenne à partir de 2035 — un accord pour assouplir cette mesure est sur le point d’être conclu entre la France et l’Allemagne. Sans surprise, Edouard Philippe, Raphaël Glucksmann et Bruno Retailleau ne partagent pas le même avis sur la question.

Le candidat Horizons considère que cette décision est une erreur. “Une stratégie, ça doit s’appuyer sur une analyse précise des moyens qu’on est capable de mettre en œuvre. Et de fait, on n’a pas été capable de mettre en œuvre ce qui aurait permis de rendre cette stratégie possible, pour autant qu’elle ait été adaptée”, a-t-il estimé lors de notre sommet. L’ancien Premier ministre plaide pour une meilleure protection du marché européen via la mise en place de droits de douane élevés sur l’importation de véhicules chinois. Une question de “réciprocité”, a-t-il martelé pendant l’entretien.

Une vision rejetée quelques instants plus tard par Raphaël Glucksmann. “Je ne vois pas du tout en quoi cet objectif [de 2035] était une erreur”, a rétorqué le tout nouveau candidat du PS et de Place publique. L’eurodéputé plaide pour que les constructeurs automobiles se concentrent sur le développement de l’électrique. “C’est ça l’avenir”, a-t-il insisté, jugeant que l’Europe a “un énorme sujet de naïveté vis-à-vis de la Chine”.

Deux positions renvoyées dos à dos par Bruno Retailleau, qui a rappelé que le groupe du Parti populaire européen, dans lequel siègent les eurodéputés LR, s’était opposé à l’instauration de cette règle lorsqu’elle a été votée au Parlement européen. “Ma position, elle est très nette, elle n’a pas changé, ça fait des années que je le demande, je dénonce cet accord”, a insisté le candidat des Républicains. Il aurait préféré voir “imposer le principe de la neutralité technologique”, via un “cadre très exigeant”, mais progressif pour les constructeurs.

Sur la question des échanges commerciaux avec Pékin, le Vendéen rejoint la position d’Edouard Philippe en s’affichant en faveur de “vrais droits de douane” sur les importations chinoises. “A partir du moment où les règles ne sont pas loyales, on doit pouvoir les compenser”, a défendu Bruno Retailleau.

Energies

Autre dissonance entre les candidats : l’énergie. Pronucléaire, Edouard Philippe a insisté sur la nécessité de “défendre” et “favoriser” l’atome, tout en ajoutant que le “risque associé à [son] exploitation” est “réel”. Si, par mesure de sécurité, il fallait interrompre la production des centrales nucléaires françaises, il faudrait que d’autres technologies puissent prendre le relai et produire de l’électricité, a-t-il exposé, mentionnant les énergies renouvelables. Sinon, la France pourrait se retrouver dans une “situation qui peut-être terrible”, a-t-il prévenu. Le candidat Horizons est par ailleurs favorable à la construction de tous les réacteurs EPR2 envisagés par l’exécutif.

Du côté de Bruno Retailleau, le discours est beaucoup plus mesuré sur les renouvelables. Le candidat LR a confirmé vouloir couper leurs subventions s’il était élu, tout comme il compte abandonner la programmation pluriannuelle de l’énergie (la PPE3), définie par le gouvernement Lecornu. Prudent, Bruno Retailleau l’est aussi sur le développement des EPR2. Alors que la construction de six nouveaux réacteurs a déjà été décidée, “on verra” pour les huit autres prévus, a-t-il temporisé.

Vision de l’Europe

Face aux menaces en matière de défense, sécurité ou IA, Raphaël Glucksmann a répondu qu’il fallait “sortir de l’intergouvernemental” et que l’Union européenne devait assumer sa puissance dans le rapport de force avec la Chine ou les Etats-Unis.

“Il faut un instrument pour les financements européens. Si vous avez des financements européens, oui, vous allez voir que subitement les projets européens fonctionnent”, a-t-il plaidé. Pour le candidat PS-Place publique, la France a tout intérêt à diversifier ses alliances en ne regardant pas seulement vers l’Allemagne, mais en se tournant vers la Pologne ou les pays baltes. “La puissance française, elle se construira dans sa capacité à construire une coalition en Europe”, a-t-il martelé.

Pour Edouard Philippe, la relation franco-allemande est “absolument déterminante dans l’ensemble européen”, même s’il ne faut “pas réduire la politique européenne” uniquement à ce duo. Selon le candidat Horizons, la France aurait tout intérêt à “être plus crédible” et à “régler [ses] sujets” (comprenez : ses sujets budgétaires et le redressement des comptes publics), si elle veut retrouver du poids politique en Europe. “Nous sommes les seuls à ne pas savoir respecter des règles communes qui ont été respectées par tous les autres. Et ça, ça nous plante”, a-t-il déploré.

La question budgétaire, c’est par cet angle que Bruno Retailleau a abordé le thème de l’UE. Selon lui, la France doit “absolument” réduire sa contribution au budget de l’Union européenne, a-t-il estimé. Le candidat des Républicains a par ailleurs apporté son soutien aux Etats membres dits “frugaux”, partisans d’un budget de l’UE réduit. “Si la France ne fait pas partie de ces pays frugaux, ça veut dire qu’on a totalement perdu contact avec la réalité”, a jugé l’ancien ministre de l’Intérieur.

Mouvement lycéen

Interrogé sur son soutien au mouvement lycéen, dont c’était “l’acte V” aujourd’hui, Raphaël Glucksmann considère que son rôle n’est pas de manifester, mais “de répondre aux revendications des lycéens et de répondre à une angoisse qui est une angoisse existentielle”. Favorable à la suppression de Parcoursup, il souhaite remplacer la plateforme par “un procédé qui est transparent, mais qui ne peut pas être le retour à ce qu’on faisait avant”, car “ce n’était pas non plus fonctionnel”, a-t-il jugé, sans donner plus de précisions.

Pour Bruno Retailleau, il ne faut pas considérer que les lycéens qui expriment des revendications dans les médias “représentent tous les lycéens”. S’il reconnaît que certaines préoccupations sont “justes”, comme “sur Parcoursup ou sur une angoisse pour l’avenir”, il oppose par exemple les revendications des lycéens ruraux aux citadins. Et note que la situation est moins bouillonnante dans une grande partie du pays.

Le candidat LR a aussi critiqué la présence de la militante écologiste suédoise Greta Thunberg devant un lycée de Seine-Saint-Denis ce matin, jugeant qu’elle incarne une “écologie dévoyée” se résumant souvent à “une forme de gauchisme”.

]]> en Lights, bells and liability: Europe’s privacy regulators crack down on smart glasses https://www.politico.eu/article/lights-bells-and-liability-europes-privacy-regulators-crack-down-on-smart-glasses/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 13 Oct 2026 14:34:37 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9152693 BRUSSELS — Privacy regulators want people wearing smart glasses in public to look and sound like a truck backing down a road.

Europe’s powerful data regulators have made stringent new recommendations on how smart glasses should alert people that the wearable devices are filming, including a combination of flashing lights, audio alerts and notifications sent to the phones of people nearby.

The European Data Protection Board (EDPB), made up of national privacy regulators across Europe, issued a statement about smart glasses on Tuesday, following a meeting in Brussels.

Privacy regulators are putting forward a united front on smart glasses, as privacy concerns about the wearable technology have multiplied since videos made with them have begun spreading online without the knowledge or consent of those being filmed.

The statement is not legally binding but will guide how privacy regulators in Europe assess whether smart glasses users and manufacturers are complying with EU privacy rules like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).

The regulators said smart glasses manufacturers should implement a combination of transparency measures to make other people aware that they are being recorded.

The measures may include lights or sounds when users are recording, requiring smart glasses users to activate them with an audible voice command, sending notifications to the smartphones of people nearby and other design “clues” to help people spot smart glasses.

The group of privacy regulators said that not only should users of smart glasses respect other people’s privacy but that the devices’ manufacturers and people providing connected apps or services may also be responsible for making sure they comply with privacy rules.

The GDPR applies to companies and organizations, and doesn’t apply when people process personal data in a household context. The regulators said this household exemption should be “narrowly interpreted” when it comes to smart glasses, and would not apply when someone shares photos or videos of others “to an indefinite number of persons on a public social media account.”

Tech firms like Meta have pitched their smart glasses to consumers on the basis that they are sleek and discreet. Meta has included an LED light in its smart glasses, which activates while recording, which it has said is a key privacy safeguard.

Samsung and Google have also recently announced that they’re collaborating on a new line of “intelligent eyewear” set to launch later this year, and Apple is reportedly aiming to hit the market with its own smart glasses by the end of 2027. 

The regulators’ statement could now force smart glasses manufacturers to reassess whether and how they sell smart glasses to European consumers. The EDPB called for industry-wide standards to be developed to make sure people are able to spot smart glasses and understand how they process data.

The European group of privacy regulators also commissioned a study into the social acceptability of smart glasses, published today.

“There is, at the head of the United States, someone who is either a useful idiot or an agent of the destruction of European strength and freedom,” Glucksmann said at POLITICO’s Competitiveness Summit in Paris. “[Russia’s war against Ukraine] targets us directly, us Europeans, and we are alone.”

The MEP also insisted that sending his far-right rival Marine Le Pen to the Elysée Palace in 2027 would be a victory for Russian leader Vladimir Putin and a step toward “the defeat of the European continent.”

Le Pen has previously expressed “a form of admiration” for Putin, and her party, the National Rally, received a loan from a Russian-linked bank in 2014. Le Pen said her party borrowed money overseas because French banks refused loans and that the loan had no impact on her political stances. The party has since paid back the funds.

Though Le Pen condemned Russia’s all-out war in Ukraine, some elected officials within her party remain strongly opposed to helping Ukraine and favor a stronger relationship with Russia.

At a POLITICO event last month, Le Pen said she believed France could provide Ukraine with military training and assistance but could no longer afford financial support given France’s budgetary constraints.

Le Pen currently boasts a double-digit lead over her competitors for the first round of next year’s presidential election, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls. Glucksmann is in fourth, trailing former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe and far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon. France’s presidential election will go to a runoff if neither of the top two candidates gets more than 50% of the vote in the first round.

In his interview with POLITICO, Glucksmann, one of the race’s strongest pro-European voices, doubled down on his support for a European Sky Shield for Ukraine and the need for a more robust, sovereign European defense industry — a push also endorsed by French President Emmanuel Macron and widely shared across the French political spectrum.

“For decades,” Glucksmann said, “we have delegated our sovereignty and our security to Washington, and we are now realizing what a mistake that was.”

In practical terms, however, Europe remains split over whether non-EU countries should be allowed to tap its defense money. France is leading the push to limit the outsiders’ access to the European Competitiveness Fund.

Glucksmann also said Europe should take on joint debt to fund defense projects — a proposal Germany and other fiscally conservative EU members have been loath to consider — instead of attempting member-state-to-member-state projects like the failed Franco-German next-generation fighter jet.

Without joint investment, he said, “no European countries, including Germany, will be able to face, in the short term, the war of the future” against powers like China, Russia and the U.S.

“It’s a life or death question,” Glucksmann said.

In a sweeping interview, Glucksmann outlined how his foreign policy, if elected president in April 2027, would involve strengthening ties with countries in central and eastern Europe instead of courting leaders like Putin or China’s Xi Jinping.

The next president, he said, “should go to Warsaw; should go to Tallinn,” rather than Beijing or Moscow. The MEP has frequently criticized Macron for hosting Putin at a lavish ceremony in the Versailles Palace in 2017 and offering Xi a tour of his grandmother’s village in southwest France in 2024.

The center-left candidate said Europe needed to “leverage its position of strength” when it comes to negotiations with China, with whom the bloc is trying to reduce its €1 billion-a-day trade deficit. He also said that the EU should stick by its goal of phasing out combustion engine vehicles by 2035 and invest in electric vehicles so as not to “abdicate” the sector to the Chinese.

Glucksmann is pitching himself to voters as a French president who will confront what he considers to be strongmen at the head of global powers like Xi, Putin and Trump.

With the presidential campaign under way, Glucksmann is also looking to strengthen his credentials on the domestic front. He said recent protests by high school students — which center, among other grievances, on the lack of substitute teachers in France, overcrowded classrooms and the run-down state of several schools — are “perfectly legitimate and justified.” He also argued that teachers are underpaid.

If not, the union has asked whether the central bank’s Governing Council received and granted an exemption. The letter also asked whether the manuscript was vetted for confidential or policy-sensitive material, and whether promoting the book at an official event was consistent with the ECB’s code of conduct.

“President Lagarde informed the ECB’s Ethics Committee and the Compliance and Governance Officer about the book project and has received approval,” the spokesperson for the central bank said.

The staff committee reminded the ECB’s compliance chief that staff rules require employees to seek prior authorization before publishing material outside their work at the central bank. The rules also restrict employees from using ECB resources, or their position, for private activities.

While ECB staff is subject to a different set of rules than the bank’s leadership, the committee said that any differences in treatment should be “objectively justified” and proportionate, the letter said, adding that ethical expectations should become “more — not less — demanding as institutional responsibility increases.”

Similarly, the staff committee wanted to know whether Lagarde had disclosed any contact with the World Economic Forum and if any potential conflicts of interest had been assessed. The ECB president is rumored to be in talks about a leadership role at the global think tank, although this has never been confirmed. 

“The book project is a private activity, carried out in the President’s own time, and does not use ECB resources,” the ECB’s spokesperson said. The staff committee declined to comment.

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Tue, 13 Oct 2026 15:47:16 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 Ukraine killing record number of Russian troops, as Putin resorts to using gangs to boost enlistment (Ukraine Battlefield update, day 1,692) https://euobserver.com/242547/ukraine-killing-record-number-of-russian-troops-as-putin-resorts-to-using-gangs-to-boost-enlistment-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1692/ Tue, 13 Oct 2026 15:47:16 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242547 Soaring Russian casualty rates and shrinking recruitment mean frontline units risk running out of men to hold or advance in Donbas, even as Ukraine keeps blowing up their supply trucks and fuel tankers.]]>
  • Russia is estimated to be recruiting 10 percent fewer soldiers this year than last, despite regions raising signing bonuses.
  • There is growing talk that criminal gangs have begun to take part in recruiting “volunteers”.
  • According to the Ukrainians, Russia is losing large numbers of soldiers, and October could be a record month.
  • Attacks on the land route to Crimea continue, reportedly prompting Russia to transport fuel in jerry cans in smaller vehicles.
  • Map of the day: Where Russia is advancing and where Ukraine is advancing
  • Videos of the day: Ukrainians hit a Russian radar; a man surfed on a Russian drone near Odesa; speculation spreads that Iran is supplying Russia with fuel.

    • Many Russians have left Russia in recent months. They feared the mobilisation that had been so widely discussed. Ukrainians said Russian president Vladimir Putin might resort to it after the September parliamentary elections. Many Russians fled to Armenia and Georgia, affecting rental prices in the capitals of these Caucasus states.

    So far, no mobilisation has taken place. Russia continues to rely on its existing system of voluntary — and, in some places, involuntary — recruitment of new soldiers in Russian regions.

    German economist Janis Kluge, who tracks regional data, wrote last week that Russia recruits around 1,000 new soldiers a day (30,000 a month). That is less than last year — down six percent in September and 10 percent over the year as a whole.

    Nor did it help that, by his estimate, the sum paid by regions as a signing bonus had risen from $16,000 (€14,000) to $22,000.

    In some places, recruitment is also beginning to move into the illegal sphere. Kluge wrote that local criminal gangs were now becoming involved in the system.

    He mentioned the case of a prosecutor in Nizhny Tagil, a city of 400,000 in the Urals. In September, he appealed to the budget committee of the local duma.

    He complained that signing bonuses for Russian soldiers were leading to an increase in crime in the city. He called for payments to agents who find volunteers willing to sign an army contract to be stopped.

    According to Kluge, the prosecutor complained that criminal elements had become involved in recruitment in the city. He said an agent received $4,500 for finding one person to sign a contract.

    Many turned to gangs to help them, with the assistance of corrupt police officers or military recruiters who are part of the scheme. “And this ‘persuasion’ may also involve violence, as another case from Sverdlovsk region shows: two criminals forced their victims to sign contracts and then seized their bonus payments,” Kluge wrote.

    In Nizhny Tagil, 580 new soldiers were recruited last year, compared with 330 this year. It is not known how many of them criminal gangs helped to “persuade” in exchange for payment. In any case, the city does not want to change its system of rewards for agents because, in the words of the deputy mayor, it helps “fulfil our tasks”.

    Overall, it is becoming increasingly difficult for Russia to supply enough manpower to the front. Moreover, it is currently losing large numbers of soldiers there, and October’s losses could even be record-breaking.

    Ukraine publishes daily figures for killed and wounded Russian soldiers. These figures cannot be verified and may be inflated, but the trend suggests that the situation is worsening for Russia.

    The table below also shows this. According to it, Russia lost around 46,000 soldiers in September — more than 1,500 a day — making it, according to Ukrainian data, the second-worst month since the start of the war. The figure was higher only in December 2024.

    This October is on course to become Russia’s worst month in this respect. By the 12th day of the month, Russia had been losing an average of 1,620 soldiers per day. If Ukraine maintains this pace, it will be a record.

    Number of Russian military casualties per month, according to Ukraine. Source: minfin.com.ua

    Naturally, the question is how much these figures can be trusted. However, the Unmanned Systems Forces, a unit commanded by Robert Brovdi, known as Magyar, also publish figures for killed and wounded Russian soldiers.

    The Ukrainian units under its command compete with one another over which can strike more Russian targets. They receive points based on this, which they can then use to buy more drones. Individual strikes should therefore be confirmed by video.

    Given this, the data published by the Unmanned Systems Forces can be considered credible. They too indicate that October could be a record month, although their data cover only one-third of Russia’s total losses.

    Number of Russian soldiers killed and wounded by SBS drones

    Record-high losses and less substantial numbers of newly recruited soldiers suggest that Russia may have difficulties replenishing its units and, consequently, advancing further in Donbas or elsewhere.

    Attacks on the land route to Crimea continue. Last week, French OSINT analyst Clément Molin published a table according to which the number of Russian lorries and trucks struck had reached a record 770. Several videos show that the number of attacks on vehicles heading to Crimea or to the front in southern Ukraine remains high. They are simply not discussed as much because this is no longer new.

    Ukraine also destroyed the Chonhar bridge, which connects Ukraine with the Crimean peninsula. Russia has used a pontoon bridge there instead. This video shows Russian cargo vehicles crossing the pontoon bridge.

    The commander of Ukraine’s 41st Pilum Unmanned Systems Regiment, part of the 1st Azov Corps, recently provided interesting information on this issue. In an interview with Radio NV, he confirmed that the number of medium-range strikes was not declining and was increasing in some areas.

    He said that the operational zone overseen by Ukraine extended from 30 to 300 km.

    According to him, Russia is trying to bring as much fuel as possible to the front. Soldiers need generators to charge equipment, power radios and drones, and keep warm.

    However, Ukrainian attacks on fuel tankers are reducing Russia’s ability to bring fuel to the front. According to the commander, in the Dobropillia direction, where his unit operates, Russia began transporting fuel in convoys this summer and switched to distributing it in passenger cars or small trucks, carrying the fuel in jerry cans.

    This does not, of course, apply to all directions. However, an ongoing stream of new videos also confirms the destruction of fuel tankers.

    Map of the day

    Russian president Vladimir Putin’s latest — though certainly not final — deadline for capturing Donbas is by the end of this year. As on 14 previous occasions, it will not be met.

    Unlike in previous years, however, it appears entirely possible that by the end of the year the territory of the free part of Donetsk region could be even larger than it is now. This is suggested by a map published by French OSINT analyst Clément Molin. It highlights areas where Ukraine is advancing and areas where Russia is pushing forward.

    As can be seen, Russian forces largely hold the initiative in the north of Kharkiv region and at one location in the south of Zaporizhzhia region.

    In the crucial Donetsk region, however, the situation is balanced; indeed, it could be said that Ukraine holds the initiative in more places. More specifically, it is clearing the northern area above Lyman and pushing further south towards Velyka Novosilka.

    Source: Clément Molin

    Videos of the day

    Ukraine’s 15th Reconnaissance Artillery Brigade published a video showing it striking a Russian 96L6 radar. This is a key component of the S-300 and S-400 air-defence systems.

    The radar can be seen moving and hiding in a tree line. Nevertheless, a Ukrainian drone struck it. It is unclear whether it was actually destroyed, as the accompanying text claims.

    A man near Odesa decided to surf on a downed Russian drone floating on the water off the coast. It hardly needs to be said that this is a fairly risky pastime. However, it indicates how at least some residents of Odesa view the daily Russian attacks.

    This could be a potentially rather interesting plot twist. The United States is at war with Iran, which has raised petrol and diesel prices at US filling stations. Donald Trump therefore agreed with Putin to import diesel from Russia. Russia itself, however, does not have enough diesel and has to import it.

    This video shows a tanker truck with Iranian registration plates in Russia. Some infer from this that Iran is importing diesel — or other fuels — into Russia, which then sends diesel to America, despite America being at war with Iran.

    However, it is too early to draw conclusions: we do not know what is in the truck or how many such Iranian tankers are heading to Russia. In any case, Russia is helping Iran in other ways.

    A Western official told Bloomberg that Russia was supplying Iran with missiles that it uses in the war against the US and Israel. It was also previously reported that Russia was helping Iran target US bases in the region.

    What are the losses:

    • By Tuesday (13 October), Russia had verifiably lost 24,192 pieces of heavy equipment (24,170 on Monday, 5 October). Of these, 19,155 (19,133) were destroyed by Ukraine, 1,002 (1,003) damaged, 1,194 (1,194) abandoned by their crews, and 2,841 (2,840) captured by the Ukrainian army. The total includes 4,453 (4,452) tanks, of which 3,358 (3,357) were destroyed in combat.
    • Ukraine lost 12,259 (12,238) pieces of equipment, of which 9,652 (9,633) were destroyed, 713 (711) damaged, 695 (695) abandoned and 1,199 (1,199) captured. The total includes 1,471 (1,466) tanks, of which 1,131 (1,126) were destroyed in combat.

    Note: Neither side regularly reports its dead or destroyed equipment. Ukraine publishes daily figures for Russian casualties and destroyed equipment, which cannot be independently verified. This overview uses data from the Oryx project, which has compiled a list of equipment losses documented exclusively by photographs since the start of the war.

    ]]>         Von der Leyen pledges more cash for Egypt and Libya regimes to keep Sudanese genocide victims out of Europe https://euobserver.com/242504/von-der-leyen-pledges-more-cash-for-egypt-and-libya-regimes-to-keep-sudanese-genocide-victims-out-of-europe/ Tue, 13 Oct 2026 14:58:26 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242504 They fled genocide in Sudan to find persecution in Egypt so they moved on to Libya, but von der Leyen aims to pay Cairo and Tripoli to keep Sudanese refugees out of Fortress EU. ]]> The European Commission is promising more support to Egypt, even as Egyptian warplanes reportedly bomb in Sudan and authorities carry out a campaign of violence against the refugees it hosts.

    The civil war in Sudan includes reports of genocide, chemical-weapons use, mass rape, and starvation, forcing some 1.2 million Sudanese people into Egypt, which was described as a priority migration-busting partner by commission president Ursula von der Leyen on Tuesday (13 October), who also promised continuing support for Cairo.

    In a letter sent to the 27 heads of state and government ahead of an EU summit on Thursday in Brussels, she spoke of “offering protection and durable solutions in … host countries”, as well as further aid for Sudanese people who had returned to parts of the country, now deemed relatively safe.

    Read more

    EU to offer Egypt more incentives at October summit

    But her warm words stand in sharp contrast to internal EU documents on Sudan, released by the London-based group Statewatch earlier this month, and which speak of an Egyptian-led campaign of violence against the Sudanese it is tasked to help.

    “The Egyptian authorities have continued arbitrary arrests, detention and deportation campaign against migrants, asylum seekers and refugees, with a sharp escalation of forced deportations being observed since January 2026,” said the Irish EU presidency, in an internal document written in September.

    Estimates suggest Egypt hosts over nine million migrants and refugees.

    Some 80 percent are Sudanese, Syrian, Yemeni, and Libyan nationals. Of those, just over 1 million are officially registered as refugees. Most come from Sudan.

    Read more

    The battle for equivalence — the EU’s role in Sudan’s civil war sanctions

    And Egypt’s crackdown also comes amid a massive 74 percent funding cut for the UN’s refugee agency in the country, even as the EU’s financial support to Cairo increases, already totalling €5bn.

    ]]>         Burnham to prioritise trade and migration at UK-EU summit, after accusing Russia of meddling in Brexit referendum https://euobserver.com/242451/burnham-to-prioritise-trade-and-migration-at-uk-eu-summit-after-accusing-russia-of-meddling-in-brexit-referendum/ Tue, 13 Oct 2026 13:34:25 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242451 The UK-EU "status quo is not good enough for Britain", claimed the British prime minister after accusing Russia of meddling in the Brexit referendum.]]> Britain is expected to push for a new post-Brexit trade deal and increased information-sharing on immigration at a UK-EU summit in Brussels next month.

    This comes as Andy Burnham, the country’s prime minister, says the post-Brexit “status quo is not good enough for Britain”, in a hint that he might seek to rejoin the European Union.

    And, more than a decade after the Brexit vote, he also accused Russia of having meddled in the 2016 British referendum.

    The UK leader will meet European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and European Council president António Costa in Brussels on 20 November.

    And Costa has also said that European and British security and prosperity are “closely intertwined”, while a closer relationship could “promote stability in Europe and beyond”.

    Made in Europe and immigration

    The November summit will be an opportunity to “raise concerns” about ‘Made in Europe,’ Burnham told members of UK MPs on Monday (12 October).

    The ‘Made in Europe’ proposal in the Industrial Accelerator Act would require companies to source a certain number of parts from within the EU to be eligible for public money in strategic sectors.

    But UK officials are worried the law could hurt British manufacturers, with Burnham expected to seek concessions.

    Read more

    Why ‘Made in Europe’ could push Burnham’s UK back into the EU’s arms

    But the British premier also wants to go further in renegotiating his country’s ties with the EU. 

    “On the table is a trade deal on food and drink products, a deal on emissions trading, progress towards linking our energy systems, a new youth experience scheme, and deeper cooperation on immigration,” he said. 

    Burnham aims to address an EU import ban on UK meat, seed potatoes, and shellfish and wants to reduce costs for shipping other goods to mainland Europe. 

    He also hopes for closer work between European and UK border forces on immigration.  

    “On immigration, we could link up our law enforcement efforts once again [since brexit], sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals,” Burnham said.

    He may aim to rejoin the Schengen Information System, a database for border management and law enforcement cooperation in Europe.

    And he could also pursue greater freedoms for UK citizens to live in the 27 member states.

    “It would be a major dereliction of duty to turn away [from the EU]” the UK leader told parliament.

    10 years on from Brexit vote

    The last EU-UK summit, held in London in 2025, was already branded as a reset in relations across the English channel, with a new defence and security partnership, reciprocal access to fishing waters, and expansion of student exchanges. 

    Read more

    Late night talks yield defence pact at EU-UK ‘reset’ summit

    And leaders are expected to build on the previous agreements by discussing defence, energy, and climate, as well as trade and migration, at their meeting next month.

    But under the terms of the EU and UK’s legal divorce in 2020, the two sides remain bound by complex limitations.

    And Burnham told MPs on Monday that renegotiating Britain’s relations with the EU could add over £10bn (€11.8bn) per year to the UK economy by 2040, “with the potential to add significantly more,” even if it did not rejoin.

    Russian meddling?

    Burnham also told a podcast on 11 October that Russia had meddled in the country’s Brexit vote 10 years ago. 

    Upon assuming office in July, Burnham asked officials if there had been Russian interference in the 2016 referendum, he told The Rest is Politics, and officials gave him a “clear answer that yes, there was.”

    “We haven’t informed people [the general public] sufficiently,” he added, amid similar Russian electoral interference in France, Germany, and further afield in Europe.

    Read more

    EU should use Digital Services Act against online tormentors of Belarusian and Russian exiles in Europe

    For his part, British foreign secretary Stephen Doughty subsequently told the LBC broadcaster: “I don’t think [Russia] succeeded in their efforts to undermine our election”.

    And Burnham also rowed back in the parliament debate on Monday when pressed by opposition MPs, by saying the outcome of the Brexit vote remained legitimate.

    But he added that Russia’s meddling in the UK’s 2019 general election was a matter of record and that it was “inconceivable that this was the first time”.

    Appetite for EU re-entry 

    Burnham also dropped hints on Monday that Britain could rejoin the European Union.

    “One thing I think is true is that public opinion has moved more quickly than political opinion. I think the political class is behind the public on this issue,” he said.

    “At every stage, the British public will be the boss,” he added, while promising a “pragmatic approach” to the hot-button issue, which has the potential to enflame right-wing anger in England.

    “We need to draw a line on a decade of drift and division [from Europe],” he said.

    But questions of a holding second referendum were “jumping ahead too far” according to Burnham.

    Read more

    Commission seeks 15-year safeguards on future member states, but says reforms won’t create two-tier EU

    The Westminster debate came after YouGov polling commissioned by Best for Britain, a pro-EU lobby group, indicated that pushing for closer EU ties would be politically advantageous for Burnham’s ruling Labour party.

    The organisation also claimed Britain could reenter the union within five years.

    Brexit was “not a sacred cow”, said Emily Thornberry, a fellow Labour MP, on Monday.

    Sandro Gozi, an Italian liberal MEP and chair of the UK-EU parliamentary partnership assembly, also said in a statement: “As a former member, and with much of the regulatory framework already in place, I personally do not see any serious reason why an application from the UK would not be achievable.”

    “When countries are already closely aligned to EU rules, such as was the case for Sweden and Finland, the process for accession is faster than for applicants essentially starting from scratch,” he said.

    ]]>         Socialist MEPs urge von der Leyen to cap methane-rules delay at one year, or withdraw it https://euobserver.com/242455/socialist-meps-urge-von-der-leyen-to-cap-methane-rules-delay-at-one-year-or-withdraw-it/ Tue, 13 Oct 2026 12:59:42 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242455 In a letter sent on Monday to commission president von der Leyen, five centre-left MEPs said any postponement must be “strictly limited to a single year.”]]> Centre-left MEPs are trying to convince the European Commission to withdraw its proposal to pause EU methane rules, if parliament or member states try to delay them for more than one year.

    Last week, energy commissioner Dan Jørgensen announced that the commission would propose delaying the import rules, due to kick in on 1 January 2027, by a year, following months of pressure from member states, the White House, and oil and gas companies.

    But in a letter sent on Monday (12 October) to commission president Ursula von der Leyen and three of her commissioners, five Socialists and Democrats (S&D) MEPs said any postponement must be “strictly limited to a single year.”

    The letter, seen by EUobserver, was signed by S&D vice-president Mohammed Chahim, Tiemo Wölken, Jens Geier, Günther Sidl, and Thomas Pellerin-Carlin.

    If parliament or member states try to push for a longer delay, the commission should “make full use of its right to withdraw the proposal,” they wrote, “as such changes would distort its purpose.”

    ]]>         Who ordered the strike that killed my friend and maimed me? The EU must demand answers from Israel https://euobserver.com/242426/who-ordered-the-strike-that-killed-my-friend-and-maimed-me-the-eu-must-demand-answers-from-israel/ Tue, 13 Oct 2026 09:26:29 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242426 I survived an Israeli strike on 13 October 2023 with one leg missing, while my friend and colleague Issam was killed. Yet three years later, no one has been held accountable. I am asking the EU to turn its commitments to protecting journalists into concrete action: demand answers from Israel and use its leverage to ensure that those responsible face justice.]]> “I’m okay.” That was the last message I sent my mother before an Israeli strike hit us, a group of seven journalists reporting in southern Lebanon.

    Three years ago, on 13 October 2023, my colleague Dylan Collins and I headed to the southern border of Lebanon to cover the situation following cross-border shelling between Israeli forces and Hezbollah. We spent the morning filming UN peacekeeping force patrols along the blue line dividing Lebanon and Israel. The atmosphere was calm and nothing suggested that the day was about to change and upend our lives. We went to a coffee shop near a UN post where journalists from different outlets had gathered and there we met our friend and Reuters colleague Issam Abdallah.

    This article is paid for by JA Europe.

    On 15 September, the European Commission proposed a Skills Portability Act, a regulation designed to make qualifications digital, comparable, and easier to recognise across borders. It forms part of the Fair Labour Mobility Package and must still be adopted by the European Parliament and the Council before any of its measures can take effect. 

    It is a welcome step. But it leaves open a question that deserves more attention in Brussels: what happens to the skills young people develop every day but their diplomas and CVs do not capture? 

    Communication, teamwork, critical thinking, adaptability and resilience shape how people work with others and keep learning throughout their careers. Employers say they need these skills. According to the Commission’s 2023 Flash Eurobarometer, 74 percent of small and medium-sized enterprises reported shortages affecting at least one job role. Meanwhile, Eurostat found that in 2024 only 56.4 percent of people aged 15–34 in the EU with medium or high educational attainment reported a high or very high match between their field of education and the requirements of their current or last main job. 

    These figures measure different things and should not be read as pointing to a single cause. Together, though, they show that having qualified people and having the right capabilities in the right place are not the same thing. Young people build those capabilities in classrooms, vocational training, volunteering, creative projects and first jobs. Yet they struggle to show them in a form that an employer, particularly one in another country, understands and trusts. 

    The stakes are not abstract. In 2025, 11 percent of Europeans aged 15–29 were neither in employment nor in education or training. Skills recognition cannot resolve that on its own, but stronger links between learning and work are part of the answer. 

    In effect, we are asking young Europeans to cross borders with incomplete passports. 

    This is where micro-credentials can make a difference if they are built with credibility in mind. JA Europe coordinates EMPASS (Employment Skills Pass), an Erasmus+ Forward-Looking Project co-funded by the European Union. It brings together education providers, industry partners and Junior Achievement organisations to develop and validate an employability micro-credential covering 11 employability skills, from communication and teamwork to resilience and critical thinking. 

    The micro-credential was designed to be piloted with 1,500 students in Greece, Romania and Spain. According to the project’s latest monitoring figures, 2,700 young people now hold an EmPass certificate. 

    Beyond the pilot, the EMPASS approach is already demonstrating potential for wider uptake. The methodology has informed implementation and exploration activities in other countries, including Ukraine and Lithuania, and has been incorporated into wider youth employability initiatives such as the Global Alliance for Youth mentoring programme. This suggests that employability micro-credentials can be integrated into different learning and workforce-development contexts while maintaining a common framework for skills recognition. 

    A micro-credential does not replace a diploma, and no single certificate can capture everything a person brings to a job. Its value lies in complementing formal qualifications with clearer, validated evidence of what someone can do. The aim should not be another certificate that employers overlook. 

    Europe does not need more initiatives that show promise but struggle to reach scale. It needs bridges: between education and employment, between national systems, and policy ambition and lived experience. That means asking practical questions. Can a young person show the same verified capabilities to employers in different countries? Can employers see what microcredential assesses and how it was validated? Can schools and universities build it into existing pathways without adding administrative burden? 

    The answers will decide whether skills portability becomes opportunity or remains a policy ambition. They are also the focus of From Skills to Opportunity, a JA Europe forum in Brussels on 14 October, bringing together policymakers, employers, educators and youth organisations, including speakers from the European Commission, the World Employment Confederation and the European Vocational Training Association. 

    As the Skills Portability Act moves through parliament and council, Europe has a chance to put employability skills into the conversation from the start: not only how qualifications are recognised, but how capabilities developed through formal, non-formal and experiential learning can carry meaning across borders. 

    Employability skills are not an abstract policy debate. They are part of the foundation for participation, mobility, and opportunity in Europe’s labour market. The task now is to ensure that every young person carries a passport that employers recognise, wherever their learning and career take them.

    This is the same area about which we have written repeatedly. For comparison, below is a map by the Russian state agency Ria Novosti. The village of Anishchyne does not appear on it, but the settlement of Vilkhuvatka — Olkhovatka in Russian — serves as a reference point in the centre-right.

    The tank and Bradley were fighting around five km north of a location that Russia marks as securely captured.

    Drones also struck Yandex’s third data centre. Graphs circulated online, particularly on Sunday, suggesting that Ukrainian attacks on Russia’s largest internet provider had restricted the operations of Russian bots around the world.

    However, this has not yet been objectively proven. Russia has indeed reported outages affecting various internet-based services after each attack, but that is so far the only confirmed effect.

    On this occasion, French analyst Clément Molin pointed out that the Russian Varyag drone brigade had attacked data centres in Ukraine in recent weeks and had boasted, among other things, of damaging Kyivstar, Ukraine’s largest operator.

    The situation has now been reversed, as it was previously with attacks on ships and warehouses. This time, however, to Russia’s disadvantage.

    The first centre hit was in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, followed by a second in Kaluga, in the Kaluga region. On Sunday, the third of Yandex’s four largest centres was struck, this time in Vladimir, in the Vladimir region.

    “This complex houses one of the company’s Galushkin supercomputers, which is among the most powerful in Russia,” Kommersant wrote, adding that the facility had been taken out of service, affecting 10 core Yandex services, including its email service.

    The situation is serious enough that, according to digital development minister Maksut Shadayev, “Yandex is facing an unprecedented attack on its data centres”.

    The defence ministry is also working on the issue in an effort to protect the company’s remaining facilities. Citing its sources, Kommersant said replacing the damaged capacity could take up to six months.

    The battle for Dobropillia on a new type of map. As the war evolves, so do the ways it is mapped. This Ukrainian OSINT profile, for example, has depicted the fighting for the important Donbas town — which protects the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration from the south-west — on a dynamic map.

    Among other things, it shows that Russian forces are infiltrating the town through the village of Hanivka from the Nove Shakhove area.

    For a clearer picture, we are also including a static DeepStateUA map, as the previous one is rotated and does not follow the usual compass orientation.

    The two maps are rotated by around 90 degrees in relation to each other. On the following one, Dobropillia is in the centre-left. Nove Shakhove, from where Russian infiltrators are advancing, is almost at the centre, exactly 10 km to the east as the crow flies. A small arrow directly next to the settlement’s name indicates the direction of Russian attacks.

    The green area in the upper part of the map is the so-called Dobropillia salient, which was fought over a year ago.

    Russia reported nothing significant concerning Dobropillia after the weekend. “On the Dobropillia axis, our forces continue to push forward, but Ukrainian units retain the ability to counterattack. Heavy fighting is under way,” the Two Majors wrote, for example.

    The Ukrainian Telegram channel Petrenko published a map over the weekend showing sites of new infiltrations. Its interpretation differs considerably from DeepStateUA’s version. Russian forces are shown closer to the town, but the direction of their advance is the same as in the two previous sources.

    The sites of the recorded incursions were established on the basis of videos showing drones killing Russian soldiers attempting to advance further west.

    Storm Shadow missiles caused the largest single massacre of senior Russian officers in August. On Friday (9 October), a joint project by Russian exile newspaper Meduza and the BBC’s Russian service added another 17,124 names to its list of Russian war casualties. This was the number it had counted since 21 September. In total, 276,113 Russian soldiers killed in the war are now known by name.

    On the same day, the project’s authors published a detailed analysis of events in Donetsk on 26 August. The Ukrainian air force had attacked a building in Donetsk with Storm Shadow/SCALP-EG missiles.

    The strike was so intense that the target must have been something significant. Almost immediately, there was speculation that the building housed an important Russian headquarters.

    Meduza and the BBC counted 20 high-ranking Russian military personnel killed during a joint meeting of the headquarters of the Centre group of forces and its subordinate 41st Army — 18 at the scene and another two from their injuries in the following days.

    They included seven colonels, six lieutenant colonels, five majors, one captain and one senior non-commissioned officer. They were identified thanks to access to nominal lists of headquarters staff as of 25 July and after that date.

    It also emerged that this was not the first time officers of the 41st Army had had a bad day. During an attack on 8 September 2025, it lost a lieutenant colonel, two majors and a lieutenant. The toll on 4 August 2026 was even worse, when the army lost two lieutenant colonels, three majors, two captains and one lieutenant at once.

    The Russian soldiers in this nighttime video appear relaxed. They were probably moving through an area they still considered relatively safe. But a waiting drone equipped with a thermal camera was tracking them.

    A Kyiv resident narrowly avoided a Russian drone at the last moment as it crashed into a playground.

    What are the losses

    No update on Friday.

    • By Monday (5 October), Russia had verifiably lost 24,170 pieces of heavy equipment (24,138 on Tuesday, 22 September). Of these, 19,133 (19,105) were destroyed by Ukraine, 1,003 (1,000) were damaged, 1,194 (1,194) were abandoned by their crews, and 2,840 (2,839) were captured by the Ukrainian army. This includes 4,452 (4,448) tanks, of which 3,357 (3,353) were destroyed in combat.
    • Ukraine lost 12,238 (12,175) pieces of equipment, of which 9,633 (9,579) were destroyed, 711 (702) damaged, 695 (695) abandoned and 1,199 (1,199) captured. This includes 1,466 (1,464) tanks, of which 1,126 (1,125) were destroyed in combat.

    Note: Neither side regularly reports its own dead or destroyed equipment. Ukraine publishes daily figures for Russian casualties and destroyed equipment, which cannot be independently verified. This overview uses data from the Oryx project, which has compiled a list based exclusively on photographically documented equipment losses since the start of the war.

    European gas storage levels are unusually low for this time of year, reaching their lowest autumn level since 2011.

    With Russian gas imports set to end in 2027, could Europe face a tougher challenge in the months ahead? 

    First, how do Europe’s gas reserves work? EU countries fill underground gas storage sites during spring and summer, when demand is lower, and draw on these stocks during the winter, when heating pushes consumption up.

    Since 2022, the EU has required member states to ensure their gas storage facilities reach 90 percent of capacity by a deadline between 1 October and 1 December. That helps secure supplies ahead of winter.

    But this year, stocks are well below that target, at just over 70 percent in early October. They still have time to rise before the deadline, but the situation is attracting attention.

    Does that mean Europeans are at risk of running out of gas this winter? According to the European Commission, no. It acknowledges that storage levels are low compared with previous years, but says the EU’s gas system should still be flexible enough to meet demand this winter.

    That said, a colder or longer winter than expected, or disruptions to supplies in other parts of the world, could put additional pressure on the market. Especially at a time when the EU is preparing to phase out Russian gas imports in 2027.

    Read more

    [Explainer] Gas glut or supply crunch? And what it means for EU methane rules

    The EU has adopted a gradual ban, with transitional arrangements for existing long-term contracts.

    Russian liquefied natural gas, or LNG, is due to be phased out completely from January 2027 only. Russian gas delivered by pipeline will follow later, with the deadline set for the end of September 2027.

    And Russian gas still accounted for around 12 percent of EU gas demand through May 2026. Imports even increased in the first months of this year compared with the same period in 2025, amid disruptions to energy flows linked to the war in the Middle East.

    So, from January, Europe will lose one source of supply.  Which means Europe should try and reduce its gas consumption.

    But it’s easier said than done, particularly as winter approaches. Heating needs depend heavily on temperatures, and households cannot simply stop heating their homes.

    Read more

    Still, Europe has shown in the past that consumption can fall significantly. After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the European Commission called on member states to reduce their gas demand by 15 percent. 

    And they succeeded: their gas demand fell of around 18 percent, compared with the previous five-year average. A few months ago, following the escalation of the war in the Middle East, the Jacques Delors Institute recommended reviving efforts to reduce gas demand.

    That being said, the reduction achieved in 2022 was partly helped by a mild winter and greater use of alternative energy sources, including coal and nuclear power.

    Those options may help again, but they come with limitations. Much will depend on the weather and how long the winter lasts.

    Which doesn’t mean Europe should not call for lowering the demand and accelerate the deployment of renewable energy.

      <title>Threat of AI share crash puts world financial stability at risk, says IMF</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/13/ai-share-crash-risk-global-imf-debt-corrowing-cyber-attacks</link>
      <description><p>High valuations and debt put sector in danger, while fund also warns on government borrowing and cyber-attacks</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/13/imf-global-economy-world-economic-outlook-uk-gdp-forecast-2026">IMF warns global economy ‘could soon test the limits of resilience’</a></p></li></ul><p>The threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets is putting world financial stability at risk, the International Monetary fund has warned.</p><p>In its twice-yearly Global Financial Stability Report, the IMF highlighted the sky-high valuations for AI companies along with their increasing debt pile as one reason that risks in the system are “elevated”.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/13/ai-share-crash-risk-global-imf-debt-corrowing-cyber-attacks">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>US economists developed models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their economies</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/live/2026/oct/12/uk-growth-inflation-pressures-oil-price-sveriges-riksbank-nobel-prize-economic-sciences-awarded-latest-news-updates">Business live – latest updates</a></p></li></ul><p>Two US economists have won the 2026 Nobel economics prize for their work developing models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their countries, avoiding long recessions and runaway inflation.</p><p>Robert Hall of Stanford University, California, and Michael Woodford of Columbia University, New York, were recognised for <a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2026/10/advanced-economicsciencesprize2026.pdf">developing the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”</a>, giving policymakers better tools to smooth out the peaks and troughs of their economies.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/12/nobel-prize-for-economics-hall-woodford-new-keynesian-models">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/11/trump-ai-economy-reagan</link>
      <description><p>‘Even if AI supercharged the economy, its impact on the government’s finances would be muted’</p><p>Back through political history to the age of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ronald-reagan">Ronald Reagan</a>, Republicans have repeatedly promised the US public that tax cuts would pay for themselves, firing up economic growth and filling the government’s coffers.</p><p>The promise never really panned out. From the Gipper’s day on, the Republicans’ tax cuts inevitably increased the budget deficit. Despite its failure, though, the promise is back, coated in a fine new layer of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/artificialintelligenceai">artificial intelligence</a> pixie dust. It will fail again.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/11/trump-ai-economy-reagan">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Order for workers to remain standing to ‘reinforce professionalism’ draws rebuke amid plunging morale</p><p>Union officials have launched a campaign to allow airport security staff to sit once more after the Trump administration unilaterally removed all the chairs for Transportation Security Administration (TSA) staff at checkpoints.</p><p>“People are pissed,” said Johnny Jones, secretary-treasurer of American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE) TSA council 100 and president of AFGE local 1040, which represents TSA workers in Dallas-Fort Worth.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/10/tsa-union-agency-checkpoints-chairs">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Trump establishes committee to investigate Fed governor Lisa Cook</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/09/trump-investigate-lisa-cook-fed-governor</link>
      <description><p>US president renews his efforts to oust Cook despite supreme court ruling that her firing was unconstitutional</p><p>Donald Trump announced on Friday that he is establishing a committee to investigate Lisa Cook, the US Federal Reserve governor, over allegations that she committed mortgage fraud, renewing his efforts to oust her despite <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jun/29/supreme-court-trump-lisa-cook-ruling">a June supreme court ruling</a> that her earlier firing was unconstitutional.</p><p>Trump said a committee will consult with justice department officials to decide whether there is “cause” for her removal. The White House will hold an in-person hearing on 5 November to consider the allegations against Cook, which will be closed to the public but transcribed and published. Cook will be able to submit a written statement to present her own evidence and will be subject to examination from White House and her own legal counsel.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/09/trump-investigate-lisa-cook-fed-governor">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Is punishing the poor Trump’s last hand to play?</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/13/trump-aca-healthcare-politics-midterms</link>
      <description><p>The pre-midterm defenestration of ACA enrollees looks like political madness – but the president appears to believe hitting poor people might work for him</p><p>There is a manic quality to <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s desperate dash to do something, anything, ahead of November’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/us-midterm-elections-2026">midterm elections</a> to convince beleaguered Americans that he can make the pressures his policies have imposed on their livelihoods go away.</p><p>The US president <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/28/trump-cattle-ranchers-beef-imports-backlash">offered</a> to lower barriers against beef imports to limit surging meat prices, only to consider <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/23/trump-beef-imports-midterms-gop-panic-01090261">backtracking</a> under <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/25/trump-republican-backlash-beef-tariff-import">pressure</a> from the cow lobby. He <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/22/trump-diesel-export-ban">offered</a> to stop diesel exports, only to find oil companies <a href="https://finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/market-chatter-us-oil-executives-112235250.html">were</a> <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/chevron-ceo-diesel-export-ban-trump-supply.html">not interested</a>. He weakened fuel efficiency standards, claiming this would trim the price of a new car (and forgetting to point out it will also raise spending on gas.) In early October he started mailing <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/01/economy/trump-obamacare-500-check">$500 checks</a> to nearly a million people touting his healthcare “wins”. Oh, and he promised adult Americans a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/10/trump-5000-midterm-cash-dividend-response">$5,000 check</a> if Republicans maintain control of Congress. That, too, will <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/10/trump-dividend-republican-midterm-convention">go nowhere</a>.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/13/trump-aca-healthcare-politics-midterms">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comTue, 13 Oct 2026 16:50:12 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[McDonald’s uses Ireland to test hand-breaded chicken in Europe]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/13/mcdonalds-uses-ireland-to-test-hand-breaded-chicken-in-europe/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/13/mcdonalds-uses-ireland-to-test-hand-breaded-chicken-in-europe/Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:34:26 +0000McDonald’s has launched a four-month “operational pilot” for hand-breaded chicken products in Ireland, the fast-food giant has announced.

Available to customers from Tuesday across a small number of Dublin restaurants, McDonald’s said the scheme “will test both the product and execution, evaluating how restaurants can deliver each menu item consistently at scale while keeping kitchen complexity to a minimum”.

“Customers will be able to enjoy hand-breaded versions of existing favourites,” the company continued, such as chicken wraps and strips. Come February, when the pilot project is set to conclude, McDonald’s plans to initiate larger-scale testing that will benefit from “advertising support”.

The Chicago-based company, which has nearly 40,000 restaurants in more than 100 countries, said it had identified a “strong customer demand” in Ireland for chicken products, complimented by “the country’s chicken leadership”.

This makes the Irish fast-food scene “an ideal market to introduce hand-breaded chicken to Europe”, McDonald’s said.

The new initiative comes as a slew of US quick-chicken brands has recently arrived in Ireland - including such as Popeyes, Wingstop, Dave’s Hot Chicken and Chick-fil-A.

Popeyes has expanded rapidly since arriving here, opening four outlets in three months.

Long may this last.

It comes as Irish household wealth has grown rapidly. In 2023, total net household wealth in Ireland was two and a half times the amount it had been just 10 years earlier, according to the report.

Although the share of that wealth held by the poorest half of households has increased in that time, almost half of all wealth continues to be controlled by the wealthiest 10 per cent of Irish households.

The structure of household wealth has also changed, the report found, with business assets accounting for a larger share “particularly among households at the top of the wealth distribution”. Further down the wealth chain, the family home continues to account for the largest share of household wealth.

The study found that, to maximise revenue, all assets outside pension funds should be taxed, with no exemptions for things like family homes, farms or businesses.

“Our wealth tax scenario analysis shows that the breadth of the tax base matters more for revenue potential than the threshold at which liability begins, with broad-base scenarios consistently generating larger aggregate tax liabilities than those with extensive exemptions,” write authors Rachel Slaymaker and Chi Tran of the ESRI and Department of Finance economists Federica De Blasio and Emmet Ryan.

Doing so, the research paper showed, would allow the tax to be set above a very high threshold where only the richest 1.5 per cent of Irish households would be affected.

It accepted that including business wealth, farms and the family home would be politically sensitive. As they are less liquid, such assets would also be harder to value on an ongoing basis.

Tax-rich Ireland at one remove from debt zeitgeist

If you allow fairly wide exemptions, the paper argued, you need to dramatically lower the threshold, bringing many more households into the wealth tax net to secure reasonable tax revenue.

The report cited the 2022 Commission on Taxation and Welfare recommendation for a gradual shift from taxing work towards taxes on wealth, capital, property and consumption, to meet the increased costs of an ageing population, public services and the climate transition, “while maintaining fiscal sustainability”.

However, it accepted that, all households, even the wealthiest could have trouble finding the cash to meet wealth tax liabilities from cash income.

Wealth taxes fell from favour in the early years of the century, the report said. Twelve European countries levied an annual tax on net wealth in 1990 but by this year, only Norway, Spain and Switzerland do so.

Limited yields, administrative and valuation difficulties, avoidance and evasion, were cited as reasons for the tax’s diminishing popularity, alongside concerns of governments around capital mobility.

Concerns around the concentration of wealth, together with pressures on public finances and the limitations of tax systems that rely predominantly on income flows, have contributed to renewed international interest in net wealth taxation in recent years.

“Recent research has increasingly emphasised that the effects of a wealth tax depend not only on whether wealth is taxed, but on how such taxes are designed,” the report said.

]]>Beeldbewerking<![CDATA[Is my €1,000 monthly childcare bill really falling to €550?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/13/is-my-1000-monthly-childcare-bill-really-falling-to-550/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/13/is-my-1000-monthly-childcare-bill-really-falling-to-550/Tue, 13 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000I pay €1,000 per month for creche (full time). What is the Budget 2027 impact here? I saw a headline suggesting childcare was being reduced to €550 per month up to senior infants but I can’t imagine that’s right. I hope so but that’s a crazy decrease.

UM

Getting your head around childcare costs can be fiendishly complex. There are different subsidies depending on your financial status and the age of the child and different bands depending on how long the child is in care.

And if it is any consolation, it is not just you and other parents who get confused. In his speech, the Minister for Public Expenditure and Reform, Jack Chambers, did say he was “reducing the maximum childcare fees paid by parents, from €735 to €550 per month for children up to senior infants”, putting €2,200 a year back into parents’ pockets.

Not quite – at least not for everyone, including you. But that does not mean there was not good news for you on childcare in the budget – at least from September of next year when the budget childcare measures kick in.

The Minister was referring to the maximum amount a parent of a child receiving between 40 and 50 hours of care a week can be charged in a creche that has signed up to the Government’s “core funding” scheme, where Government subsidises the cost of care. This is called Band E.

If you are paying €1,000 – or more accurately €959 – a month, you will be in Band F, where your child is receiving care for more than 50 hours a week.

And you are far from alone in having been taken aback by talk of the €735 and €550 maximums.

The Minister’s team insist that Band E is the one most commonly used by parents across the State. That may be so; the statement was not accompanied by figures. What does seem certain is that most parents in Dublin and some surrounding commuter counties, as well as areas of Cork and Galway, are paying Band F fees like you.

Budget 2027’s childcare package has triggered storm of protest from parents. Here’s why

The net cost to you is determined by two things: fee per band and the personal subsidy to which each child is entitled, depending on your income.

Under the budget measures, the fee for Band F will fall from €336 a week to €300. And, for those on the universal subsidy (anyone with family income of more than €73,000), the subsidy for children up to senior infants will rise to €2.50 from €2.15 per hour up to a maximum of 45 hours.

If your income is below €73,000, the subsidy may be higher and, if it is below €36,500, that could be as high as €5.10 an hour.

When they say household income, they mean income minus any pension contributions you pay. You also do not include certain welfare payments and, if you have more than one child, there are further income disregards.

Anyway, back to the numbers. That €2.50 an hour universal subsidy amounts to €112.50 a week. Taking this from your €300 “fee”, you are left with €187.50. From September next year (11 months in the future), that will be your weekly fee, amounting to €750 a month.

That means a fall of at least €209 in your childcare cost per child each month, or somewhere between €2,300 and €2,500 over the year. So good news, if not quite a drop in charge to €550.

Of course, that is only if you are in a creche that operates under Government core funding. If not, they are free to charge what the market will bear.

]]>Heather Diehl<![CDATA[The signs are AI prefers AI-written CVs, and one law firm’s experience is revealing]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/12/what-if-ai-prefers-cvs-written-by-ai/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/12/what-if-ai-prefers-cvs-written-by-ai/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000Earlier this year, in the depths of summer, the Addleshaw Goddard law firm found itself in a slight pickle.

The problem was, the longer it took to sift them, the higher the chance that good candidates would find work elsewhere. Like a lot of organisations, Addleshaw has been encouraging its managers to test ways that AI can safely improve its processes, so the firm’s HR department decided to do an experiment. It would see how well an AI agent could assess the applications compared with humans.

An agent was duly set up, using the firm’s internal Microsoft Copilot system, and told about the role that needed to be filled, as well as the experience applicants would need with certain HR systems and programming languages, and with AI itself.

Humans at the firm sorted the applicants into a shorter pile of about a dozen and asked the agent to score them.

The agent whipped through this task and presented a list of what it deemed to be the top contenders. The humans did the same thing.

Alas, the two lists did not match. The agent was impressed by glossy applications from candidates who claimed to have achieved exceptional IT feats in record time at a previous employer, or worked on big projects despite scant levels of experience. In short, they were too good to be true – and smacked of having been written with the help of AI.

Who’s hiring and who’s firing in Ireland’s technology sector?

Katherine Rathbone, Addleshaw Goddard’s head of HR, told me her team had theories about why this might have happened.

For one thing, AI tools can make it a lot easier for candidates to tailor a CV to match a job description. But that was not all. “One possible explanation is that, because AI capability was itself one of the criteria, the agent may have interpreted signs of AI use in producing the CV as evidence of AI capability,” she said.

There is another, more disturbing possibility. The AI agent may have actively preferred CVs purely because AI was involved in writing them.

If so, it would confirm the findings of an eye-catching working paper that has analysed the behaviour of AI hiring tools.

The researchers simulated what they said were realistic hiring processes for 24 jobs ranging from teachers and consultants to chefs and engineers.
