Harris, who would be chairing discussions during the EU presidency, had gone back and forth with his advisers about tying himself to a firm date. Ultimately they decided it would help put the pressure on everyone.

The Council of the EU is the body where the member states, either at the level of officials, ambassadors, or ministers, shape policy coming from Brussels. The “presidency” rotates from country to country every six months, and for that period you are expected to be a neutral broker, steering the debate towards a common compromise.

Political agreement had long proved elusive when it came to reforms of the EU’s capital markets.

EU governments agree on long-stalled capital markets reform

The idea has been knocking around for a long time – a very long time in fact.

“Though a European capital market ought to be the result of spontaneous developments, it will nonetheless require constructive efforts on the part of governments and financial institutions,” Italian economist Claudio Segré wrote in a 1966 report for the then-European Economic Community (ECC).

An expert group chaired by Segré, a commission official, said creating a “broad” European capital market made good economic sense.

Brussels officials took a proper stab at it in the years that followed the financial crash.

Jean-Claude Juncker, then-European Commission president, spoke about creating a “capital markets union” in 2014. The changes would involve greater regulation at EU rather than national level, and aligning things such as insolvency regimes and other financial rules.

Building on banking reforms in the post-crash period, the president of the EU’s lawmaking body said the changes would “increase the attractiveness of Europe as a place to invest”.

Ireland’s EU presidency proposes budget cut of €141bn for the bloc

Everyone agrees in principle, but individual national capitals had traditionally been nervous that they would lose out in the shake-up.

France has been a big fan of the plan. That’s no surprise given the reforms would expand the remit of the existing European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), which is based in Paris.

Ireland and Luxembourg, two small member states with big financial services sectors, eyed plans to hand extra powers over to a European regulator with great suspicion.

The pair had teamed up in the past to oppose a shift towards a souped-up European regulator, fearing companies and firms would be tempted to set up shop in Paris in the future, rather than Dublin or Luxembourg.

Concerns about Europe’s sluggish economy, and a creeping sense the EU was falling further behind the United States and China, reignited the debate.

A 2024 report by another Italian economist, Mario Draghi, said the EU needed to push through the long-stalled capital market reforms to jump-start growth. The former European Central Bank chief warned the alternative would be a slow, painful economic decline.

EU’s big six push to centralise financial oversight in move that will worry Ireland

Breaking down national barriers that were stopping capital and investment from flowing throughout the 27-state union was key to that, Draghi said.

Ursula von der Leyen rebranded the capital reforms the “savings and investment union”, part of which would significantly expand ESMA’s remit to oversee financial markets.

The sprawling piece of complex legislation, the Market Integration and Supervision Package was kicked on to the member states, to see if they could land a deal everyone could live with this time.

Securing that deal by a self-imposed October deadline was ambitious but doable, Harris wrote in a letter to his fellow finance ministers after a meeting in July.

There was broad support around the room to get the thing done, subject to the shape of compromise.

A huge amount of the heavy lifting took place in Brussels at official-level.

A working group, chaired by Irish finance attache Emma Moyles, met more than a dozen times in the following months to knead out the sticky details. Department of Finance colleagues in Dublin were heavily involved too.

Irish negotiators got an honest sense of the red lines and the space for a “landing zone” in separate one-to-one discussions with officials from each of the other member states.

When talking to fellow finance ministers, Harris often mentioned Ireland didn’t need unanimous support to approve a deal, only a qualified majority of EU states, a much easier bar to clear.

A compromise text was drafted and redrafted by the Irish presidency that ran to several hundred pages.

The reworked proposal, seen by The Irish Times, included several big changes aimed at bringing reluctant countries around.

The confidential text shows Luxembourg secured leeway in the oversight of asset management groups. Malta opposed ESMA taking over the regulation of crypto platforms, so European oversight was limited to large platforms.

More broadly, representatives of national authorities and central banks would retain a role in ESMA’s governance too.

It was the carveout to accommodate the Germans that kicked off the biggest storm.

We have achieved more in the last 10 months than we have achieved in the last 10 years

Eelco Heinen, Dutch finance minister

Deutsche Börse Group, who run the Frankfurt Stock Exchange, would not come under the supervision of the EU-level authority, but remain regulated locally.

The German government argued the carveout was justified on the basis Deutsche Börse only operates in Germany, rather than across EU borders. BME, who run the Spanish Stock Exchange, were also exempt from ESMA oversight, following lobbying by Madrid.

Several member states, and the commission, were unhappy with the way Germany bagged an opt-out for its stock exchange, while others were being pressed to hand over decision-making authority to a European supervisor. “If we are doing this, we have to do it altogether,” said a diplomat from one country annoyed at the German carveout.

“If it’s a German sausage at the end of all this, what’s the point of it,” one industry source remarked, a reference to the ugly business of policymaking.

Belgium complained about the need to have a “level playing field”. The Belgian government had unsuccessfully pushed for Euroclear, a major central securities depository in its back yard, to remain regulated at national level.

Ambassadors from each member state, who are their governments’ eyes and ears in Brussels, picked up the debate last Wednesday.

Several sources briefed on the closed-door discussion said about 10 member states intervened to register their annoyance. The European Commission were also frustrated the ambition of the reforms had been “significantly” watered down.

Harris wants deal on contentious EU capital market reforms by October

Officials continued to negotiate deep in the weeds of the massively technical package of reforms, as finance ministers made their way to Luxembourg for their October 9th meeting.

A dinner had been arranged the evening before, where Harris again made the case. They could all spend another six months debating the finer points and they’d probably be in the same position, he said. “No compromise is perfect,” he told the room.

By breakfast the following morning, it seemed clear the other ministers agreed. Word filtered out shortly after they took their seats for the actual EU council meeting: deal done.

“We have achieved more in the last 10 months than we have achieved in the last 10 years,” Dutch finance minister Eelco Heinen later said.

All member states – bar Belgium who abstained – voted to back the compromise crafted by the Irish presidency, faults, carveouts and all.

That’s not the end of things though. MEPs in the European Parliament will have a chance to amend the package, before national governments give their final sign-off.

Speaking at a press conference afterwards, Harris cautioned against waiting around and letting the perfect become the enemy of the good. “That’s not how the European Union works,” he said.

]]>AILBE PHOTO<![CDATA[Budget reversal of policy on tackling climate change was a mistake]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/12/budget-reversal-of-the-policy-on-tackling-climate-change-was-a-mistake/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/12/budget-reversal-of-the-policy-on-tackling-climate-change-was-a-mistake/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000There are three crucial tasks for any budget: does it implement a long-term economic strategy; is the trajectory of the public finances sustainable; and will it manage aggregate demand in the economy so that economic activity remains close to capacity?

This year the strategic priorities for the Government should be to enhance the economic security of the State and promote long-term growth, tackle climate change, and reduce poverty, especially child poverty.

The budget has further increased our dependence on corporation tax as indirect taxes are reduced, increasing the economy’s vulnerability. However, unlike many other economies, we will still run a small surplus next year; it is just that it should be much larger.

This budget scores well on growth, committing increased resources for infrastructural investment. Government investment, which is €20 billion this year, will increase by almost 15 per cent in 2027. This is more than 5 per cent of national income, much higher than in other countries, reflecting our rapid population growth.

Some of this investment will go on the start-up of MetroLink and other projects, but the fruits of this investment will only be fully apparent many elections hence. Jam today would have been easier for the Government, but this is the right answer.

Where the budget is faulty is the reversal of the policy on tackling climate change. The carbon tax was due to rise gradually to 2030 to encourage us to reduce emissions and to fund investment in key climate projects, such as retrofitting and protecting those on low incomes. This budget has reversed this, cutting the tax rate on certain fuels, with a commitment to leave it at this low level to 2030. This sends all the wrong signals, and it also means there will be significantly fewer resources to protect those who are energy poor and to fund important climate investment, including flood protection.

The number of children in poverty is increasing, despite our run of economic success. Research by the ESRI has shown that the best way to tackle this problem would be to introduce targeted income supports for children living in low-income families. An opportunity to do this was missed last week.

Dealing with the effects of higher inflation on living standards is best done in a number of ways. The income tax system should be indexed so that the tax take does not increase by stealth. In contrast to last year, this budget does this.

The exceptionally high energy prices pose particular problems for those on low incomes, with higher expenditure on heating. This clearly needed to be addressed, and the best way of doing it would have been to increase welfare payments and introduce targeted support for the energy needs of the most vulnerable.

The Government won’t raise carbon tax again but promises to decarbonise the economy – how?

Instead, Government expenditure on social payments will rise by only 2.7 per cent next year, less than inflation, and there is no significant targeted support for those who need it most.

More of the reduction in excise tax on fuel goes to those on high incomes, reducing the incentive to cut our emissions of greenhouse gases. None of it goes to those who cannot afford a car. An unsatisfactory outcome for the climate, and for those on low incomes who will suffer from the cold this winter.

If the Government sticks to the numbers in the budget it looks likely that it will be neutral, neither stimulating nor deflating the economy. While some tightening would have been better, the stimulus largely arises from the very desirable increase in public investment.

The budgetary numbers published last week also show the share of public expenditure in national income next year will remain roughly unchanged compared to this year. If this proves to be the outcome, it would be satisfactory. However, as with recent budgets, this one carries the seeds of another overrun.

It is no surprise that Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers did not put a precise number on the provision for public service pay next year. He is beginning a negotiating process, and anything he provided would be taken just as the starting point by trade unions. Thus, there is likely to be some overrun to provide for the final outturn of the pay talks.

The provision for social payments looks like an underestimate of what will be spent. Also, once again in some departmental budgets, it looks as if the estimates do not provide for expenditure that will prove unavoidable, for example in health.

While on paper the budget numbers look moderately prudent, as in previous years, they may prove a poor guide to the eventual outturn.

]]>Paul Faith<![CDATA[More needs to be done to help home-grown companies scale and offset reliance on FDI]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/more-needs-to-be-done-to-help-home-grown-companies-scale-and-offset-reliance-on-fdi/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/more-needs-to-be-done-to-help-home-grown-companies-scale-and-offset-reliance-on-fdi/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 04:31:00 +0000Ireland’s economic model has been one of the great success stories of modern Europe. Our multinational sector has transformed employment and public finances. But we have come to a point now when what made us stand apart feels a little less different and we need to look at future-proofing our economy.

At the same time, Ireland’s private sector continues to underperform when it comes to scaling indigenous companies into globally competitive multinationals. Ireland needs to enhance its offering to FDI as well as putting measures in place to help its home-grown businesses scale into global companies.

Ireland’s corporation tax receipts rose from €4.7 billion in 2014 to €32.9 billion in 2025, now accounting for about 31 per cent of total exchequer tax revenue, compared with just 8.3 per cent in 2014.

This concentration is more than 2.5 times the OECD average (12 per cent). Revenue analysis shows that foreign-owned multinationals generate almost 90 per cent of these receipts, while the three largest companies accounted for 46 per cent of all corporation tax paid in 2024.

While it is unlikely that there will be a significant reduction in corporation tax receipts over the next few years, the picture is far less certain over a 10- to 15-year horizon. The challenge for policymakers is that decisions about future investment are being made today. If Ireland waits until corporation tax receipts begin to decline before responding, it may be too late to attract the next wave of investment required to sustain our spending commitments and economic success. The Government needs to act now.

There are several ways Ireland can enhance its offering to international companies as well as doing more for home-grown private businesses.

Firstly, Ireland needs to invest now for the future. This is not simply about protecting existing industries; it is about identifying the sectors that will drive economic growth in the decades ahead and putting the policies, infrastructure and incentives in place now to attract them.

Ireland should be reinvesting part of today’s corporation tax revenues to develop domestic businesses, support innovation and secure the next generation of FDI. The objective should be clear: act while the tide is still coming in, not after it has turned.

Secondly, Ireland needs to become a more compelling location for high-value research, development and innovation activities. The current R&D tax credit, despite small enhancements in Budget 2027, would benefit from expanding the range of activities covered.

State’s tax take boosted by €3bn as multinationals ‘front-load’ payments

The relief should be expanded to increase the benefit for advanced manufacturing investment opportunities. Budget 2027 missed an opportunity to introduce a separate innovation incentive for broader innovation activities, supporting investment in areas such as digitalisation and decarbonisation. These reforms would strengthen Ireland’s attractiveness as a global innovation hub while further supporting private companies.

Thirdly, too many promising private businesses are acquired before they reach scale. Irish firms face systemic barriers that limit their ability to grow and scale. Three things are needed to help – capital, capabilities and culture.

The Government has begun to recognise the capital challenge through its proposed €1 billion Scaling Fund announced in Budget 2027. This is a welcome start, but much will depend on the accessibility of funds. Scaling an Irish business towards a public listing should be more attractive and achievable – Euronext Dublin has only about two dozen actively traded equities, compared with nearly 2,000 listed companies across European markets.

The introduction of the State investment account is also a welcome step towards mobilising pools of capital in Ireland, with the potential to channel significant household savings towards active investment and broaden participation in capital markets. The next challenge is ensuring that a meaningful proportion of those funds is channelled into promising Irish companies, helping to create the next generation of indigenous businesses.

While the budget announcement to reduce Capital Gains Tax to 31 per cent is positive, a larger reduction to 20 per cent would have gone a lot further towards encouraging further investment. Furthermore, revised entrepreneur relief should be enhanced and retirement relief expanded.

Irish businesses need the talent, leadership and expertise to help them scale from successful start-ups into global enterprises. The announcement of funding to the National Training Fund to build skills and resilience fit for an AI-enabled workforce was a practical step and a sign that the State can provide supports to nurture these capabilities. But more of this is needed. Finally, Ireland must create a culture that rewards ambition, celebrates success and makes scaling indigenous businesses a national priority.

Budget 2027: Measures put public finances on worse trajectory, State watchdog warns

Not every competitiveness issue requires money. Often, smaller businesses face administration burdens that consume valuable time and resources without delivering meaningful economic benefits. Simplification has minimal cost to the exchequer but can have a significant impact.

For example, in our pre-budget submission, we suggested pre-populated simplified tax returns for small businesses. The budget move to allow enhanced reporting requirements to be submitted monthly rather than on a real-time basis is a welcome step. However, there remains a strong case for moving to an annual reporting requirement.

The announcement of a holistic assessment of the various grant schemes, enterprise tax incentives and business development programmes now on offer will hopefully lead to meaningful simplification. However, this will only truly deliver impact if a cross-departmental approach is taken, as success is measured by a reduction in form-filling and hours saved processing applications.

Ireland does not need a completely new economic model. The foundations of our success remain strong. However, maintaining success in a changing world requires enhancing our offering to FDI and the private sector – reinvesting for competitiveness. The real question is whether we are prepared to invest today in what will make us attractive tomorrow.

Paraic Burke is head of tax at PwC Ireland

]]><![CDATA[‘Politeness premium’ costing Irish consumers €600m each year, research suggests]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/politeness-premium-costing-irish-consumers-600m-each-year-research-suggests/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/politeness-premium-costing-irish-consumers-600m-each-year-research-suggests/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000Irish consumers lose an average of €150 each year as a result of a “politeness premium” which sees them overpay on shared bills and fail to collect personal debts, according to research published by AIB on Monday morning.

The study suggests that fewer than one in 20 Irish adults will always ask for money they are owed back, with as many as 90 per cent saying they would let as much as €50 slide rather than have a conversation they consider difficult.

All told, about €600 million gets lost to social awkwardness every year, AIB said.

And as if to prove the Shakespearean wisdom about never being either a borrower or a lender, the unspoken debt has “soured a relationship” among almost 50 per cent of those surveyed.

The research also highlights how consumers handle peer-to-peer debts varies dramatically depending on county, age and gender.

The geographical divide in financial assertiveness indicates that people from Galway have Ireland’s highest ‘threshold of asking’ and willingly absorb up to €32.50 in unpaid amounts before speaking up.

By contrast, people living in Wexford draw the line much earlier by refusing to let more than €12.50 slide.

Adults from Limerick are the most likely to insist on itemising group bills line by line, while those living in Dublin prefer splitting bills evenly among the group.

When asked why they hesitate to chase small debts, Irish adults often frame their silence as kindness and say things such as “they’d do the same for me”, “it evens out over time”, or “I’d rather be generous than keep score”.

Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: How does it work if I have €1 or €12,000 to put in?

However, behavioural data reveals the underlying tension when payments arise, with 40 per cent saying owed money left unspoken has soured how they feel about a relationship and two thirds admitting to a level of discomfort when someone suggests itemising a group bill.

Nearly half said they regularly overpay on shared bills or rounds to keep the peace, with 25- to 34-year-olds feeling the greatest pressure and 74 per cent overpaying regularly, according to the survey of 1,009 adults conducted by Bounce Insights on behalf of AIB and Ogilvy.

Close friends and colleagues were deemed to be the hardest groups to ask for money back from, with women saying they found it particularly difficult to reclaim money from close friends.

“People rarely describe their silence around money as awkwardness,” said Dan Bennett, global head of behavioural science with Ogilvy Consulting. “They describe it as generosity. But the cost of that politeness is real, showing up both in people’s bank accounts and in their relationships. In Ireland, the fear of appearing impolite leads many of us to pay a ‘politeness premium’.”

“The behavioural science research that AIB’s new Everyday Banking campaign is rooted in highlights how social dynamics impact our daily finances, create social friction and can even cost people money,” said the bank’s chief customer officer Orlaith Ryan.

]]>MilosStankovic<![CDATA[Ireland goes Swedish on investment, but deemed disposal remains a problem]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/12/ireland-goes-swedish-on-investment-but-deemed-disposal-remains-a-problem/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/12/ireland-goes-swedish-on-investment-but-deemed-disposal-remains-a-problem/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 03:01:00 +0000Earlier this year, Stocktake suggested Minister for Finance Simon Harris might be tempted to borrow Sweden’s model for encouraging people to invest.

It turns out he was. The Savings and Investment Account (SIA) announced in Budget 2027 is not a carbon copy of Sweden’s ISK, but the resemblance is clear.

Investors can put up to €12,000 a year into the account, with the first €50,000 of investments exempt from tax, while amounts above that will face an annual 1 per cent charge.

Some will be irked by that charge, especially in years where stock markets have fallen. However, a UK-style tax-free wrapper, allowing savers to invest up to £20,000 a year completely free of tax, always appeared excessively generous and politically indefensible.

For the Government, a Swedish-type approach offers a predictable tax stream while encouraging people to put their savings into shares and funds (and a €50,000 tax-free limit is more generous than many expected) rather than leaving them in cash.

However, the new account also highlights the problem with the system outside it. Investments held in the SIA will escape deemed disposal, while investors buying ordinary ETFs will continue to face an eight-year tax charge on unrealised gains, albeit at the reduced rate of 35 per cent.

The Government says it intends to move beyond deemed disposal during the lifetime of this administration, but substantive reform has again been deferred.

And there is a second, less discussed problem. The Funds Sector 2030 review recommended limited loss relief, but the Government’s roadmap says it will not be introduced. As Stocktake previously noted, an investor who makes €5,000 on one ETF and loses €5,000 on another can therefore have no overall gain but still face tax on the €5,000 profit.

Is the State’s new investment account going to be a good deal?

That is less of an issue for someone holding one broad global ETF, but it matters for a portfolio of separate funds.

Some will have issues with the SIA, but it’s arguably a welcome attempt to make investing simpler. The harder task is making the wider investing tax system equally sensible.

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3444929/">
   <title>Unis und ÖH warnen vor Kürzungen</title>
   <description>Bis Ende Oktober muss laut Gesetz feststehen, wie viel Geld die öffentlichen Unis für ihr nächstes Dreijahresbudget ab 2028 erhalten. Am Wochenende will die Regierung die Summe fixieren. Die Universitätenkonferenz (uniko) befürchtet wegen der Einsparungen im aktuellen Doppelbudget Einschnitte von rund einer Mrd. Euro bis 2030 und warnt vor einem großen Stellenabbau. Die Österreichische Hochschülerinnen- und Hochschülerschaft (ÖH) rief erneut zum Protest auf, die Unis unterstützten die Aktion.</description>
   <link>https://orf.at/stories/3444929/</link>

   <title>Indische Polizei nahm mehrere Anführer fest</title>
   <description>In Indien hat die Polizei am Dienstag mehrere führende Vertreter der „Kakerlaken“-Partei (CJP) festgenommen. Sie hatten zuvor Absperrungen am historischen Observatorium Jantar Mantar in der Hauptstadt Neu-Delhi überwunden. Zu den etwa 20 Festgenommenen gehörten drei führende Mitstreiter, erklärte der Gründer der Bewegung, der jüngst selbst zwischenzeitlich festgenommene Abhijeet Dipke.</description>

    <item>

Poland and Norway have signed a declaration on deepening security cooperation, including joint defence production, strengthening NATO’s northern and eastern flanks, and continuing to support Ukraine.

“In a world where the international order, laws and principles are being violated by the world’s biggest players, Poland and Norway show how partnership can be built on shared values and interests,” said Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, alongside his Norwegian counterpart, Jonas Gahr Støre.

🇵🇱🤝🇳🇴 Strategiczne partnerstwo Polski i Królestwa Norwegii oficjalnie przypieczętowane.

✍️ Podpisano deklarację o strategicznym partnerstwie między obu państwami, stanowiącą efekt wieloletniej współpracy oraz wspólnoty interesów biznesowych, geopolitycznych i moralnych.

🛡️ W… pic.twitter.com/vBrWrdC8oT

— Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 12, 2026

The two leaders signed a declaration on strategic partnership during a visit by a Norwegian delegation to the Warsaw Security Forum, where Norway is this year’s partner country. The agreement sets out a framework for closer long-term cooperation between the two countries.

Among the commitments made by the two countries are “deeper operational cooperation” and expanding joint procurement and production between their respective defence industries.

Warsaw and Oslo also pledged to work together on strengthening NATO’s eastern and northern flanks, as well as to coordinate responses to cyberattacks, hybrid operations and foreign information manipulation.

“The point is that Europe should take on greater responsibility for security,” said Støre. “We must invest in it more coherently and consistently, so as to avoid duplication, but invest in such a way that regional defence systems are stronger.”

 

The declaration also promises continued support for Ukraine in its defence against Russia, as well as efforts to ensure a just and lasting peace and to “hold Russia accountable for its war of aggression”.

Although security issues dominate the declaration, the two countries also pledged to deepen economic ties, including in the energy and maritime sectors.

Robin Allers, a scholar at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that the move to sign the declaration with Poland was part of a broader Norwegian strategy to deepen mutual commitments with key NATO partners amid uncertainty over US engagement in Europe.

“Today’s agreement demonstrates your country’s increasingly important role in Europe,” said Allers, pointing to Poland’s growing economic and military strength, as well as its role in supporting Ukraine.

Poland has unveiled its first frigate to enter service in decades at a ceremony in the Baltic port of Gdynia, where the ship was constructed.

It will be followed by two more new frigates as part of a €3.5bn programme to modernise the ageing Polish fleet https://t.co/093Fx2WSM7

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026

Poland has in recent years also moved to strengthen its ties with countries around the Baltic Sea. This year, Polish and Norwegian companies announced plans to develop a new anti-drone system for Poland in the wake of incursions of Russian drones into Polish airspace.

Last year, Norway opened a facility in Poland, Camp Jomsborg, for training Ukrainian military personnel. In January, it was announced that Poland will manufacture missiles for rocket artillery systems that Norway is purchasing from South Korea. Norway has already bought Piorun air-defence systems from Poland.

The two countries also have close energy ties. In 2022, the Baltic Pipe began delivering Norwegian gas to Poland, helping the country reduce its reliance on Russian supplies. Norway’s Equinor is also involved in developing one of Poland’s first offshore wind farms in the Baltic.

Poland will manufacture the missiles for rocket artillery systems that Norway is buying from South Korea.

The Norwegian government says that Polish production "will strengthen security of supply for Norway and other European customers of the system" https://t.co/NIJj7owK45

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 29, 2026

Poland has also moved closer in recent years to Sweden, with which it signed a strategic partnership in 2024. The two countries subsequently held their first bilateral military exercises in the Baltic, and Poland this year ordered three submarines from Swedish manufacturer Saab.

Last year, at Poland’s suggestion, NATO launched a new military mission to protect critical infrastructure in the Baltic Sea.

On Monday this week, Norway’s defence ministry announced that Poland will join an initiative recently launched by 11 European countries and Canada to cooperate more closely on security in the North Atlantic, Arctic and Baltic Sea.

Two Turkish men suspected of carrying out last month’s arson attack on a satellite internet ground station in Poland used by Starlink have been detained in Germany. The Polish authorities say that the sabotage was carried out on behalf of Russia.

On Monday evening, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk first announced that the pair had been taken into custody “at the request of the Polish security services”.

He said that the Turkish men’s actions had been “a further act of hybrid warfare” – the term used for sabotage and other hostile activity carried out in Europe by Russia – and that “the perpetrators will answer before the Polish justice system”.

Na zlecenie polskich służb niemiecka policja zatrzymała dwóch obywateli tureckich podejrzanych o podpalenie stacji Starlink na Mazowszu. To kolejny akt wojny hybrydowej. Sprawcy sabotażu odpowiedzą przed polskim wymiarem sprawiedliwości.

— Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 12, 2026

Shortly afterwards, interior minister Marcin Kierwiński revealed that the arrests had taken place in cooperation between Poland’s police and Internal Security Agency (ABW) and Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA).

He said that the charge the suspects are likely to face in Poland would be “sabotage on behalf of a foreign intelligence service”, a crime that carries a minimum prison sentence of 10 years, ranging up to life.

Later on Monday, Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of the security services, confirmed that Poland believes the attack was carried out “on behalf of the Russian security services”.

 

The incident in question took place on 23 September at a ground station in Poland used by Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite internet company. The facility is used to provide internet services across the region, including in Ukraine, which has relied heavily on Starlink connections since Russia’s full-scale invasion.

Firefighters were called out that evening to a fire at the facility, which is owned by Polish state telecommunications operator Exatel. The next day, digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gakowski revealed that the blaze had been started deliberately and “the modus operandi is clearly Russian”.

Poland has been one of the primary targets for Russian sabotage operations in Europe. Those have included a series of arson attacks, including one that burned down Warsaw’s largest shopping centre and another at a drone factory that is used to supply the Ukrainian military.

A fire last night at a Starlink ground station in Poland that is used to provide internet services to Ukraine was caused deliberately and "the modus operandi is clearly Russian", says digital affairs minister @KGawkowski https://t.co/p2DEn7XexF

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 24, 2026

On Monday evening, at a press conference alongside Kierwiński and Siemoniak, the commander of Poland’s police, Marek Boroń, revealed that one of the two Turkish suspects had resident status in Germany while the other did not.

He said that the Polish authorities had been able to document their movements in Poland, and had recordings, fingerprints and DNA of the suspects.

Simoniak added that there was a “high probability” that other individuals were involved in the attack, but that he could not divulge further information about them currently. He also thanked the German authorities for their cooperation.

“We have no doubt that Russian intelligence services are behind this act of sabotage,” said the minister, quoted by the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. “And it’s worth adding that Russian intelligence services are increasingly using people connected to the criminal world. They never use their own citizens.”

Russia uses individuals already present in Europe – and often already involved in criminal activity – to carry out most of its hybrid operations. On Monday, in a separate case, three Ukrainians and one Belarusian went on trial in Warsaw accused of being behind a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania.

Four men – three Ukrainians and a Belarusian – have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on behalf of Russia https://t.co/i4czRb9DYZ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026

On Tuesday morning, German newspaper Handelsblatt reported confirmation from the State Criminal Police Office (LKA) in Baden-Württemberg that two Turkish men had been detained on Monday in the town of Nürtingen at the request of the Polish authorities.

The office did not provide further details, but Handelsblatt reports that the two suspects are due to be brought before a judge today.

]]> Four go on trial in Warsaw over arson attacks carried out on Russian orders https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/12/four-go-on-trial-in-warsaw-over-arson-attacks-carried-out-on-russian-orders/ Mon, 12 Oct 2026 13:25:22 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=103850

Four men have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders.

The accused – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – can be named only as Oleksandr H., Stepan K., Vitalii K. and Pavlo T. under Polish privacy law and their trial is taking place behind closed doors for security reasons.

Polish prosecutors say that they were part of an organised group tasked with “committing acts of sabotage and terrorism” on behalf of Russia’s foreign intelligence service in April and May 2024.

Those included a fire that burned down Warsaw’s largest shopping centre, Marywilska 44; another at a store in Warsaw belonging to home improvement chain OBI; and a third at an IKEA store in Vilnius. They also allegedly planned an arson attack on an IKEA store in the Latvian capital of Riga.

W Sądzie Okręgowym Warszawa-Praga ruszył proces grupy przestępczej, która miała na zlecenie Federacji Rosyjskiej podpalać markety wielkopowierzchniowe, w tym centrum handlowe przy Marywilskiej w Warszawie.https://t.co/0CFl1RyJvq

— TVN Warszawa (@tvnwarszawa) October 12, 2026

According to an indictment issued against the men in March this year, Stepan K., the Belarusian, set fire to the OBI store. Oleksandr H. is accused of involvement in the arson attack on the IKEA store in Vilnius and preparations for further attacks.

The pair have been indicted under Poland’s espionage law for carrying out acts of sabotage and terrorism on behalf of foreign intelligence. That crime carries a minimum sentence of 10 years in prison, ranging up to life.

Another Ukrainian suspect, Daniil B., had also been due to stand trial today on the same charge, with prosecutors finding that he had received an order from a handler in Russia to go to Marywilska on the night the arson attack took place and record footage of the fire and the response of the emergency services.

However, Daniil B. was jailed in Lithuania last year for his role in the Vilnius IKEA fire and Poland has not yet managed to secure his extradition for the trial in Warsaw, meaning that it went ahead without his involvement.

Polish prosecutors say they have determined that the Marywilska fire was also carried out on the orders of Russian intelligence, but have not been able to identify which individuals actually perpetrated the attack.

 

Stepan K. and Oleksandr H. – as well as Vitalii K., whom prosecutors accuse of helping carry out the arson in Vilnius – are additionally charged with participating in an organised criminal group that aimed to carry out terrorist offences, a crime punishable by up to 10 years in prison.

Both Vitalii K. and Pavlo T. were also indicted in relation to an assault in the village of Wólka Kosowska, just outside Warsaw.

Pavlo T. was already convicted in Poland last year along with two other Ukrainian men, Serhii R. and Vladyslav Y., over their role in the same criminal group tasked with carrying out acts of sabotage and terrorism by Russia. They were handed jail terms ranging from 16 months to five and a half years.

Two other alleged members of the group, Serhii Chalyi and Oleksandr Varyvoda, who prosecutors say were involved in coordinating sabotage activities, remain wanted.

Three Ukrainians have been jailed in Poland for their role in a group tasked with carrying out sabotage and terrorism.

That included the fire that destroyed Warsaw’s largest shopping centre, which Polish prosecutors say was carried out on Russia’s orders https://t.co/xuFx5T4HH9

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 24, 2025

In response to evidence that Moscow was behind the Marywilska fire, Poland last year ordered Russia’s consulate in Kraków to close. It has since closed all Russian consulates due to Moscow’s ongoing campaign of sabotage, with Russia responding by shutting down all Polish consulates on its territory.

A report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published earlier this year found that Poland is the “primary focus” of Russian sabotage in Europe.

Most recently, Poland has accused Moscow of being behind a fire at a drone factory that supplies the Polish and Ukrainian militaries. Last year, Ukrainian operatives working on behalf of Russia also used explosives in an attempt to derail a train in Poland.

Most acts of sabotage ordered by Russia in Poland have been carried out not by Russians themselves, but by Ukrainians and Belarusians, large numbers of whom already live in Poland and other countries in the region.

]]> Israeli producer had access to data harvested by Poland using Pegasus spyware, say prosecutors https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/12/israeli-producer-had-access-to-data-harvested-by-poland-using-pegasus-spyware-say-prosecutors/ Mon, 12 Oct 2026 12:27:25 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105380

Data harvested from mobile phones by the Polish authorities using Pegasus spyware were transmitted outside Poland and were accessible to the tool’s Israeli producer, Polish prosecutors have revealed as part of an investigation into the use of Pegasus under the former government.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk says that the case is “one of the biggest scandals in Polish history since the fall of communism”, and that it is “beyond any doubt” that the Israeli firm behind Pegasus, NSO Group, cooperates with Israeli intelligence.

Tego o Pegasusie jeszcze nie słyszeliście. pic.twitter.com/etvhTE9EWa

— Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 12, 2026

Pegasus is a powerful and controversial tool that allows the extraction of large amounts of data from mobile phones without users’ knowledge. A number of countries have been found to have used it to spy on opposition figures.

In 2017, Poland, under the government of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, purchased Pegasus from NSO. The spyware was subsequently used against hundreds of targets, including a number of PiS’s political opponents.

Among them was the head of the 2019 election campaign of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party (which was then known as Civic Platform, PO). Last year, Tusk revealed that his own wife and daughter had been among those caught up in the surveillance.

PiS, however, has insisted that Pegasus was a necessary tool to fight crime and ensure national security. It says the spyware was only used with court approval against targets legitimately suspected of wrongdoing.

 

After a coalition led by Tusk took power from PiS in December 2023, it launched investigations into the use of Pegasus under the former government.

Today, the National Prosecutor’s Office released its latest findings, based on analysis by experts at the forensic research office of Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW).

The experts confirmed that Pegasus allowed the harvesting of emails, instant messaging and text messages; the content of telephone conversations, both via mobile networks and internet calls; browsing histories, calendars and contact lists; photos, videos and other files; and location data.

“Additionally, Pegasus allowed the use of the device’s built-in microphone and cameras to record audio and video in real time and take screenshots,” reports the National Prosecutor’s Office.

Czy to możliwe, że państwo traci kontrolę nad własnym systemem inwigilacji? I to nie była stara konsola…

Z opinii biegłych ABW wynika, że CBA kupiło narzędzie, nad którym nie miało pełnej kontroli. Dane opuszczały Polskę, moduł infekujący kontrolował producent, a zagraniczna…

— Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) October 12, 2026

The ABW experts also highlighted serious concerns over management and security of the harvested data, noting that Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA), which was responsible for using the spyware, “did not have full control over the Pegasus system”.

“The CBA did not have passwords to access some accounts with administrative privileges and some system components remained under the control of the manufacturer [NSO],” wrote the prosecutor’s office. “The server module responsible for infecting mobile devices remained under the manufacturer’s exclusive control.”

Data transmitted through the Pegasus system travelled outside Polish territory, through “servers located in various parts of the world”, in a network managed by NSO and “beyond the CBA’s control”, found the experts.

Meanwhile, NSO “had technical access to materials from operational surveillance”, although prosecutors say that the experts “did not determine whether the manufacturer actually obtained access to materials from specific operations”.

The former deputy head of Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau has been charged with unlawfully sharing material obtained through surveillance using Pegasus spyware, including communication involving PM @donaldtusk's daughter when Tusk was in opposition https://t.co/LyTuqbq0KQ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 23, 2025

In a video commenting on the latest findings, Tusk said that the investigation into Pegasus was “coming to a head”. He called it “one of the biggest scandals in Polish history after the fall of communism”.

The former PIS authorities signed a contract for a spyware system “over which they de facto had no control, because control remained in the hands of Israel and an Israeli company…whose cooperation with Israeli intelligence is, of course, beyond doubt”, said the prime minister.

“They paid money for a system that de facto transferred all possible data on Polish citizens, Polish opposition leaders and Polish independent prosecutors…to the Israeli side,” he added. “This is no longer [just] a scandal…We’re talking about a crime against the state.”

Two former heads of Polish security agencies have been charged over the use of Pegasus spyware under the former PiS government.

The pair, who deny wrongdoing, could be jailed for up to three years if found guilty of unlawfully allowing use of the spyware https://t.co/TWjQR74IYT

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 26, 2026

Later on Monday, a separate parliamentary committee set up by the ruling coalition to investigate the use of Pegasus also revealed unclassified sections of a report on its findings.

In addition to the information released by prosecutors, the commission also said that the CBA had never obtained the required IT security accreditation for Pegasus, meaning that it was used without meeting requirements for protecting classified information.

The commission’s chairwoman, Magdalena Sroka, also said that courts granting authorisation for the use of Pegasus were not informed of its full capabilities, such as the ability to access the entire contents of phones, reports broadcaster RMF.

💬 Jest to dokument o tym, jak władza publiczna w Polsce sięgnęła po narzędzie ingerujące w prawa obywatelskie – powiedziała przewodnicząca komisji śledczej ds. inwigilacji systemem Pegasus @MagdalenaSroka, prezentując raport z prac komisji.https://t.co/MzA9gj4M0Y

— PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) October 12, 2026

Legal proceedings are already underway against a number of former officials in relation to Pegasus. In February, prosecutors charged the former heads of the AWB and Military Counterintelligence Service (SKW) with abuse of power for approving the use of Pegasus despite being aware of legal shortcomings.

Previously, the former head of the CBA was charged with the same offence, while one of his deputies was charged with unlawfully disclosing material from surveillance of Roman Giertych, an MP from Tusk’s KO party who has also worked as a lawyer for Tusk and his family.

Last year, a former deputy justice minister from the PiS government, Michał Woś, was indicted to stand trial over his role in the alleged illegal use of justice ministry funds to help the CBA purchase Pegasus.

The case involves two Bangladeshi nationals and one Indian, all legal residents in Poland. The incident came to light in December 2025, after witnesses reported seeing the trio leading a goat through the centre of the city of Wałbrzych, before taking it to the back of a kebab bar.

After killing the animal, the men began butchering it for meat, which they were still portioning out when the police arrived. They told officers that the meat was intended for their own consumption. The kebab bar was closed for renovations at the time.

The men also said that such slaughter was customary in their home countries and they were unaware that, with limited exceptions, animals in Poland may generally be slaughtered only at authorised slaughterhouses, reports broadcaster RMF

 

A spokesman for prosecutors, Mariusz Pindera, told the Wirtualna Polska news website that the men’s unfamiliarity with Polish law did not “absolve them of the obligation to comply with the regulations”.

Prosecutors have therefore asked the court for a so-called conditional discontinuation of the case, a very common procedure under Polish law. Almost 25,000 such motions were submitted last year by prosecutors, citing the low social harm of the offences involved, reports Wirtualna Polska.

The court must now decide whether to accept or reject the prosecution’s motion. In the latter case, prosecutors would be required to proceed with an indictment against the suspects and seek a conviction. No hearing date on the motion has yet been set.

A sign installed to warn the public about damage caused by beavers has been destroyed by the beavers themselves, according to the Polish foresters who erected it.

The incident was reported in a post on social media by the forestry district of Lubliniec in southern Poland, which shared photos of the sign, which read “Warning! Damage caused by beavers”. The wooden post it was displayed on had been destroyed in an apparent beaver attack.

“We wanted to warn you about the potential consequences of beaver activity at the pond and the surrounding area – since beavers dig burrows under the road and fell trees near the pond – but the beavers didn’t want you to be warned, so…they cut down the oak post displaying the hazard notice,” wrote the foresters.

“So, if you are around the pond, please exercise caution; and if you spot a piece of wood sticking out of the ground that has been gnawed by beavers, just imagine there was a sign there reading ‘Warning! Damage caused by beavers’.”

Beavers were once almost hunted to extinction in Poland. By 1928, it was estimated that only 235 remained in the country. However, thanks to postwar efforts to reintroduce the animals into the Polish wilderness, the beaver population has grown and is currently estimated at around 150,000.

Ecologists note that beavers play an important role in tackling drought by retaining water through the dams they build. Those dams also create “oases of biodiversity”, notes the state water agency PGW WP.

However, the rodents can cause damage to roads, houses and farmland, which has led some to call for culls to keep beaver numbers down.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:28:03 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.0.7 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 ‘Expect to be spied on’: MI5 chief warns UK tech startups over foreign threats https://www.cityam.com/expect-to-be-spied-on-mi5-chief-warns-uk-tech-startups-over-foreign-threats/ Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:06:36 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2465467

British tech startups should expect to be targeted by foreign spies, the head of MI5 has warned, as the security service ramps up efforts to tackle cyberattacks and the growing national security risks posed by AI. Sir Ken McCallum, director general of MI5, has urged British businesses to strengthen their cyber defences, warning that hostile [...]]]>

British tech startups should expect to be targeted by foreign spies, the head of MI5 has warned, as the security service ramps up efforts to tackle cyberattacks and the growing national security risks posed by AI.

Sir Ken McCallum, director general of MI5, has urged British businesses to strengthen their cyber defences, warning that hostile states were increasingly targeting the UK’s tech sector and critical infrastructure.

“If you’re a tech start up, expect to be spied on by foreign actors and sort your cybersecurity”, he said in his annual threat update at Thames House.

McCallum warned that Britain’s financial systems and supply chains were increasingly vulnerable to attacks designed to cause maximum disruption.

“Our interconnected financial systems, energy grids, supply chains and manufacturing bases, designed during simpler times for maximum efficiency, are vulnerable to malicious disruption and coercion”, he said.

He pointed to a destructive cyberattack on a UK energy generator, warning that the consequences of such incidents could extend directly to consumers.

“A hack of your banking app could lock you out of your accounts”, he said. “A cyber attack on your local hospital could delay your treatment”.

MI5 launches new AI threat unit

The MI5 chief also revealed that the agency had launched a new AI Threat Assessment Centre (AITAC), bringing together expertise from the AI Security Institute, National Crime Agency and National Cyber Security Centre.

The unit, housed within MI5, will assess emerging threats from AI as intelligence agencies race to keep pace with increasingly sophisticated technology.

“Today AI is already supercharging the cybersecurity contast between attackers and defenders”, McCallum said.

He warned that terrorists were already attempting to exploit AI to improve their reconnaissance and attack methods, while the technology could also generate personalised propaganda and radicalising material.

“We’ve caught terrorists seeking to exploit AI to improve their reconnaissance and attack methodologies, with AI-enabled drones adding a new twist”, he said.

McCallum identified the potential development of biological weapons ass one of his greatest concerns, although he stressed that the threat had not yet materialised”.

“Not yet realised – but the misuse case to which I’d attached greatest weight – is AI’s potential to change the stakes on existing or even new bioweapons”, he said.

His intervention comes amid mounting concerns over foreign attempts to obtain sensitive British tech and research.

Last month, MI5 warned that over 100 UK-linked academics had contributed to projects funded by a Chinese institute allegedly connected to Beijing’s intelligence services.

The agency said the China General Technology Research Institute had funded research into AI and cybersecurity designed to strengthen China’s espionage capabilities.

McCallum referenced the warning on Tuesday, saying Chinese intelligence had been using research partnerships to target British expertise.

The MI5 chief also revealed that the agency’s state-threat caseload had quadrupled over the past decade, with more resources now devoted to countering hostile states than during the Cold War.

He warned that Britain had entered a new era of national security in which businesses and individuals could no longer assume they were insulated from geopolitical threats.

“In this new world, we should expect to be tested”, he said.

ASCOT’s British Champions Day this Saturday provides a final chance for some of the stars of the Flat season to strut their stuff before the campaign winds down.

On a star-studded card, the aim is to hunt out a bit of ante-post value and take on the many short-priced favourites set to line up.

There are races where you can’t follow that policy, however, and I do think CALANDAGAN can win the Group One Champion Stakes (4.00pm) for a second year running.

Francis Henri-Graffard’s five-year-old was so impressive in this contest 12 months ago, when he powered clear of Ombudsman to win by over two lengths.

Arriving here fresh last year saw him produce one of his best performances and, given a similar preparation this time, I can see this French raider repeating the feat.

The ground at Ascot might not be as soft as it can be at this time of year, but I expect it to be on the slow side of good come Saturday.

Autumnal good ground can still be hard work, but Calandagan proved he can get through it last year, and I’m not so sure it suits his main market rival Ombudsman as much.

Hotazhell and Almaqam make some each-way appeal, but I expect Calandagan to once again stamp his class on this contest and the 5/2 around is fair.

William Haggas’ Almeraq will be a banker for many in the Group One British Champions Sprint Stakes (2.05pm), and that would be especially true if more rain arrives.

This is a race that can produce a shock, as was the case 12 months ago when Powerful Glory returned a 200/1 winner, and there have also been winners at 40/1, 33/1 and 28/1 in the last 10 years.

With that in mind, I’m happy to take a chance on two at each-way prices.

The first is another Haggas horse in DIVISION, who is probably a bigger price at 10/1 than he would be if his trainer didn’t also saddle the market leader.

This horse has some excellent form to his name, including when beaten less than a length into third in the Commonwealth Cup over this course and distance.

It didn’t look as though he was ready for his most recent run at Ascot earlier this month, having been given a break since August.

He still finished his race off well to be fourth though, and, with that run behind him, he should do better on Saturday.

Given the form he has shown, GREAT WISH looks a big price at 14/1.

This son of Night Of Thunder has won his last two races, including when destroying his rivals by over four lengths in a French Group Three last time.

It’s also worth remembering he was only just over two lengths behind Almeraq when they met at Royal Ascot this summer.

He’s likely such a big price as he’s trained by Danish handler Bent Olsen, and I’m happy to take the inflated odds.

Kalpana looks likely to cap a brilliant season for trainer Andrew Balding as she bids to defend her Group One British Champions Fillies & Mares Stakes (2.40pm) crown.

While it takes a bit of imagination to see past her, I do think Johnny Murtagh’s BELIEVED is interesting at 20/1.

She ran a fine race to be a close third behind Enceladus in the King George V Stakes at Royal Ascot, and last time out won a Group Three at Cork.

She’s clearly improving and, being owned by the day’s sponsors Qatar Racing, she should be primed to go well.

Football regulator boss David Kogan has vowed to quit if prevented from punishing Manchester City’s owners — and is ready to ask government for extra cash to fight any legal challenge from Abu Dhabi. The Independent Football Regulator has the power to disqualify City’s owners and force Sheikh Mansour to sell up following the club’s [...]]]>

Football regulator boss David Kogan has vowed to quit if prevented from punishing Manchester City’s owners — and is ready to ask government for extra cash to fight any legal challenge from Abu Dhabi.

The Independent Football Regulator has the power to disqualify City’s owners and force Sheikh Mansour to sell up following the club’s conviction for systematically breaking Premier League rules.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has raised concerns about that outcome, prompting fears of government interference, but Kogan has made it clear he won’t stand for ministerial meddling. 

“Our independence is absolute, and my independence personally is absolute,” said Kogan, who previously donated to the Labour leadership campaigns of Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy and Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer. 

“I made it very clear last year that any form of political interference in the way we operate is going to result in my resigning from this role, and I stand by that completely. 

“To be crystal clear, we’ve come under absolutely no political pressure whatsoever on this or any other topic, and I don’t expect to in the future. I think ministers and indeed opposition parties know full well that we’re going to act entirely independently.”

The IFR will wait for City’s appeal against more than 100 convictions of financial rule-breaking before taking any action, which Kogan said would be based on legal advice.

IFR will demand more funding if sued by Man City, says Kogan

If disqualified, Sheikh Mansour would be given a deadline to sell which, if not met, would trigger a third party taking over the sale at a price City would have no control over.

“We are not a black and white, tick-box regulator,” said IFR CEO Richard Monks. “It allows us to take a broad view of the suitability of a particular owner.”

Kogan dismissed concerns that the IFR did not have deep enough pockets to sustain long-running legal action from super-wealthy owners such as City’s, saying it would demand more money from the government in order to fight its case.

“If we’re facing a long-running legal challenge, we will clearly go back to government and get financial support from government. That’s nothing to do with our current budget. That’s going to be an exceptional circumstance,” he added. 

“I don’t expect a problem with the Treasury or with DCMS if we’re suddenly facing a substantive legal challenge, assuming that legal challenge is one that we’re prepared to fight and prepared to win. But as I say, we have yet to face that situation.”

State of the Game report and New Deal close

Kogan and Monks were speaking in Manchester at the launch of the draft State of the Game report, which will inform its policy and, they said, highlighted the dichotomy between English football’s great success and growing financial risks.

A major step towards resolving that – a new deal that will see more money flow more evenly from the Premier League to the divisions below – now appears close after years of wrangling. “I think the leagues are pretty much agreed on most of the detail,” Kogan said.

The IFR will take a more proactive approach to clubs seeking to exploit loopholes in financial rules by, in the case of Chelsea, selling their women’s team to a related party or, in several others, selling their stadium or other assets to their ultimate owner.

“If a club tried to do something like that under our regime, we would just say no,” said Monks. “We wouldn’t just say no in terms of pointing to a specific rule, but because we have this much broader assessment of risk.” Monks added the regulator could instead allow it but insist on other measures, such as clubs trebling their cash balance.

The IFR will next week reveal its plans for the levy on clubs which will fund its costs and those incurred by government in establishing the watchdog. Any extraordinary legal action it is required to fight would not come from its levy-derived budget, Kogan said.

It isn’t typically a film’s duty to push a political agenda, but with Artificial, the biopic of OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman, there is a clear call to action. It is inevitable that people will ask: ‘What can this film do?’ 

Luca Guadagnino’s eleventh film is a particularly disturbing portrait of AI, following the tech entrepreneur Sam Altman, who launched AI chatbot Chat GPT in 2022, instigating an arms race involving Grok, Gemini, and Claude. Some leading scientists have claimed that the power and potential of these programmes means they could destroy humanity by the end of the 2020s.

A decade ago that would have been the stuff of science fiction movies, but in autumn 2026, Artificial feels terrifyingly prescient.

You hang on the every word of this grounded professor, particularly as employees learn that AI gaining sentience doesn’t necessarily mean it’ll be better than humans, rather it will be flawed like us.

At the same time, the UK’s AI minister is warning of an “inevitable” AI attack on the country. The number of ISA millionaires in the UK hit a record high, as more Brits chose to plough their cash into the tax-shielded account.

The total number of stocks and shares ISA millionaires increased by more than 50 per cent in the 2023/24 tax year, reaching a record 7,730 according to an FOI request from financial app Plum to HMRC.

This marked a further 2,660 Brits holding £1m or more in their ISA accounts, up from 5,070 in the 2022/23 tax year, and represented the largest year-on-year increase since 2016.

According to HMRC data, the average ISA millionaire was holding a pot worth roughly £1.3m in April 2024. 

Around 60 savvy savers had pots worth around £4m, while the top 25 investors had accounts averaging an eye-watering £11.9m.

Patient investors

Stocks and shares ISA allows individuals to invest in the stock market without paying tax on profits. The product has grown in popularity in recent years as both the government and financial industry have raised awareness of the benefits of moving away from cash savings.

“These aren’t people who suddenly saved their way to £1m. It’s the result of years of patient investing, where the growth on your growth starts doing the heavy lifting. That’s the bit people underestimate,” said Will Bryant, director of wealth strategy at Plum.

“These figures underline the value of investing and the importance of taking a long-term approach. Despite the geopolitical volatility of recent years, global markets powered by the U.S. stock market have continued to climb.”

Tax system upheaval

Bryant also pointed towards the benefit of allocating capital into an ISA as families brace for pensions to be pulled into the scope of inheritance tax (IHT) from April 2027.

ISA pots remain exempt from IHT if passed onto a spouse or civil partner.

The cash ISA ceiling is also set to be slashed from £20,000 to £12,000 from the next financial year, while the stocks and shares ceiling is set to remain at £20,000 in a bid to get more people to opt to save into the product.

Bryant said: “The ISA reforms may lead people to use more of their stocks & shares ISA to make full use of their tax-free allowance.”

Figures released by HMRC in September showed around £135.7 billion was subscribed to adult ISAs in the tax year 2024/25, a £32.7 billion annual increase.

Meta has challenged the UK regulator in court over how it calculates fees and fines under the UK’s online safety law, as it argued the methods are disproportionate and unlawful.

The tech giant has questioned the media regulator, Ofcom, over its definition of ‘qualifying worldwide revenue’, which it uses to calculate financial penalties and fees for tech companies which earn over £250m a year.

The parties are at a judicial review hearing in the English High Court on Tuesday and Wednesday.

The regulator created and drafted the Qualifying Worldwide Revenue (QWR) provisions in September last year under the Online Safety Act, which introduced new protections against harmful online content. Under the rules, firms found to have breached safety rules can face fines of up to 10 per cent of qualifying worldwide revenue or £18m, whichever is the higher amount.

Under the new rules, if Ofcom enforces against a single entity owned by a tech firm, such as a social media platform, it will calculate financial penalties based only on that entity’s revenue.

However, if the regulator enforces against multiple entities, including a firm’s parent company and subsidiaries, it can instead calculate the amount based on the group’s total revenue generated from everything, including non-regulated activities such as enterprise software.

According to court filings seen by City AM, Meta has alleged the Online Safety Act does not give the regulator powers to include revenue for non-regulated services when pursuing multiple entities, and so Ofcom is breaching its own statutory powers and “acting irrationally” by creating a “double counting” approach to calculating fines and fees.

The US tech firm is claiming Ofcom deliberately adopted the “broadest possible approach” of those rules to grant itself power to impose financial penalties on providers “at an unprecedented level of magnitude.”

Ofcom, however, argued that Meta “is incorrect” and that it “struck a careful balance” in adopting its approach to calculating financial penalties.

“A fundamental flaw with this argument is that it was no part of the purpose of the QWR Regulations to set the ‘level’ of any penalty. The QWR Regulations determine the methodology for calculating the maximum penalty in a particular case, but Ofcom will determine the appropriate and proportionate level of penalty on the facts of the case at hand,” Ofcom said in court filings seen by City AM.

In a statement, a Meta spokesperson said the tech giant is “committed to cooperating constructively with Ofcom as it enforces the Online Safety Act.”

“However, we and others in the tech industry believe its decisions on the methodology to calculate fees and potential fines are disproportionate. We believe fees and penalties should be based on the services being regulated in the countries where they’re being regulated. This would still allow Ofcom to impose the largest fines in UK corporate history,” the spokesperson said.

An Ofcom spokesperson said in a statement: “Parliament has charged us with the job of regulating an industry that has been unregulated and unaccountable for more than 20 years.”

“Effective regulation relies on our ability to gather information, levy appropriate fees, issue fines and apply the law as intended. While legal challenges are an important part of any regulatory regime, we will defend them robustly as part of our mission of making life safer online for people in the UK.”

Regulator ‘operating in a highly litigious environment’

During a meeting for the House of Lords Communications and Digital Committee on 15 September, Ofcom’s group director for online safety, Oliver Griffiths, said the regulator is “operating in a highly litigious environment” as it is facing two lots of legal proceedings brought by Meta over its fee calculation, amongst other online service providers bringing similar claims.

Griffiths added the regulator has “a raft of services that are bringing judicial reviews against us for trying to collect data so that we can monitor and evaluate what is happening” with the online safety regime.

The Midday Market report is a new newsletter from City AM, giving you fresh analysis on the biggest stories in the City straight into your inbox every lunchtime. Today, Ali Lyon weighs up what Tuesday’s IMF report says about the state of the UK economy. Sign up to the City AM News Updates newsletter here.

To read this morning’s World Economic Outlook from the IMF is to be left confused about the state of the UK economy.

The dollops of good news – and there certainly were a few – were without fail accompanied by caveats and qualifications. Where we were singled out for praise, economists from the pre-eminent monetary authority quickly brought us back down to earth with a thud.

We are – if you’ll allow me to lean on a rather tortured analogy – in the top quartile of our class. Our academic performance – 1.3 per cent GDP growth this year and 1.2 per cent next – is solid if by no means remarkable. And our behaviour – a promise to balance the books (excluding investment) by the end of the parliament – is positively gold-star worthy.

But that good end of term report is made a lot less impressive when one considers that almost everyone else in the class is, by the IMF’s reckoning, on the brink of being put in special measures. And that the teachers’ comments for us left quite a bit of room for improvement.

It was a paper teeming with interesting and politically dicey contradictions. One long do-you-want-the-good-news-or-the-bad-news assessment. But there were three big paradoxes that are worth singling out.

The Great British Paradox in the UK economy

Growth – but make it hot:

Let’s tackle the two big-ticket items up top. We are on course to have the second-fastest growth of any major European economy both this year and in 2027. Given that the IMF’s last global economic temperature check warned we were especially exposed to the then-nascent Iran war, those real GDP numbers can be chalked up as a success. We have proven to be much more resilient than many expected.

But while we’re all enjoying the spoils of our economic unexceptionality, we will also be fighting to contain the second-highest inflation of any developed economy, the IMF warned.

Prices will rise by an average of 3.3 per cent this year, and are on track to jump by a further 2.8 per cent in 2027, assuming the Middle East war dies down by around March, as the report’s authors have.

In short, the UK is looking relatively growth-y. But our exposure to external events – be that via our poor food security, our ideological energy system or our embarrassment of hyper-regulated industries – means we’ll have to get used to higher prices for longer than our counterparts.

Our fiscal position is better than most – but vulnerable to slippage:

Authors singled the UK out for its ambitious deficit reduction targets, which are the most ambitious and impressive of any G7 economy. Speaking at a press conference, IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro praised our “consolidation path”, which official targets say will see us bring tax revenue back in line with day-to-day spending by 2029/30. That is considerably lower than the yawning deficits on show in countries like France and the US, which were both placed firmly on the IMF’s naughty step.

But she also raised a gentle eyebrow as to just how realistic our goals are given the rather expensive-sounding mood music coming out of 10 (if not 11) Downing Street. “The message for the UK is simply: stay the course,” Tenreyro said. “And continue on that trajectory.”

Bifurc-AI-tion in the UK economy

As one would expect, AI, and how it will uproot the global economy, was a theme throughout the IMF’s big barometer. The technology’s rapid development helps explain much of why the Middle East conflict has not taken an even larger chunk out of countries’ GDP figures. That is particularly the case in the UK economy, where our abundance of white-collar, professional industries allows us to adopt AI – and its economic uplift – faster than many others.

The kicker (there was always going to be one, wasn’t there) is that once that initial adoption is over, we are among the most exposed of any developed country to its disruptive impact. Our high energy costs preclude us from developing frontier models here almost entirely. We can’t point to any meaningful cottage industries – be they chipmakers, designers and the like – to boost our enormous trade deficit. And, most disconcertingly, there is the small issue of what happens if all those white-collar workers who are currently leaning on the tech for their productivity are suddenly not needed at all.

That worrying notion notwithstanding, there are plenty of positives to take from our bi-annual MOT from the world’s monetary authority. If it really were a report card, it would likely read, “Some good work done this term by the UK economy – but come 28 October, it can’t afford to let itself down at its first big exam.”
